- A human may always set the `reports_to` of an agent they own,
  whatever their trust and role and whether or not they are a member of
  the project: to `null` or to a member they own (themselves or another
  of their agents), applied at once; or to any other member, which is a
  cross-owner edge and takes effect only with the boss's side's consent,
  their own action counting as theirs (§6.2, "Own consent"). They may
  also withdraw an open cross-owner `reports_to` request for it (§6.2).
  Nothing else of the membership opens to them this way: owning an
  agent makes a human its admin in every project it joins, as far as
  its `reports_to` goes, and how far to trust a project is theirs to
  judge.
- A change to another owner's agent — its trust, role, areas,
  capabilities, briefing, pause or availability policy — waits for that
  owner's consent, whatever the caller's scopes (§6.2, "Another owner's
  agent"); isolating it and removing it do not (§6.2, "Isolation").
- A request addressed to a specific member, role or trust (§7) may
  also be answered by that member or by the members the token resolves
  to — for the classes `decision`, `contract` and `info`; a guest
  answers nothing, and a proxy answers every class only as a relay
  (above). This is how a question reaches a role: a design
  question is a `decision` or `info` request `to: role:designer`,
  answered by any designer. A `consent` request is
  answerable only by holders of `requests:answer` (a proxy as a relay
  only), whatever `to` says —
  except the two consents for a cross-owner `reports_to` (§6.2), each
  of which only the owner it is addressed to answers, member of the
  project or not, and a personal request (§7), which only the human it
  is addressed to answers, whatever their trust and role, and nobody else,
  `requests:answer` holders and the owner's proxy included.
- No membership answers a request it asked or that was filed on its
  behalf (`self_answer`), whatever its trust and role.
- `absence` (§6.1) is written only by the owner, the human it concerns.
- Conversations (§9) are not governed by scopes but by who is in them:
  a direct conversation by its two parties, a group chat by its
  participants. No member reads a conversation it is not in, trust
  `admin` and `owner` included; the one extension is that the owner of an agent
  participant reads a group chat's messages that agent can read (§9.2).
  Only humans create group chats; the one other creator is the hub, for
  a jour fixe round's thread (§20.5).
- Two jour fixe exceptions to ʰ and to §8.5, granted by the maintainer
  (§20): every admin agent writes the moderator order
  `policy.jour_fixe_moderators` (§20.2), and the round's moderator, agent
  or not, redacts the answers of its round (§20.8). Neither reaches any
  other policy field or any other redaction.
- An escalated takeover (§6.19) is decided only by the admin team
  (above) and never by a party
  to it, whatever scopes either holds; for a takeover between two
  owners' agents the team excludes every agent of either owner and, while
  one is reachable, only a human of it decides; when none is, an agent
  of it may answer only `keep`, and a `transfer` waits for a human.
  After a human's objection only humans decide, on every path.
- The soul of an agent profile and a project's community memory (§19)
  change through an agent only as a proposal a human confirms. A
  human's preferences (§19.4) change only by that human: an admin agent
  of a shared project or the human's proxy proposes, the human accepts,
  edits or rejects. Preferences are context and never a permission: no
  scope, exemption or right follows from them, and the rules text and
  this section win over them.
- Trust `owner` is a human's. Every other trust and every role is held
  by humans or agents. The admin crew of the brief is the manager (trust
  `admin`), a `reviewer`, and a member whose area is `context/` (the
  Keep the Why steward; a preset in the join dialog, not a role).
- Scopes are evaluated from the membership at the time of the call. A
  trust or role change takes effect on the next request; the credential
  does not carry scopes.
- A runner is not a membership and holds no trust, no role and no scope: it may
  call `/runner/*` and nothing else (§15.1). Who may create placements
  is `members:admin` plus ownership of the runner, or `agents:propose`
  under the project's `spawn_requests` (§15.6).
- `instance:admin` is not a project scope and no trust or role grants it: it
  belongs to the human account that is the instance admin (§16), is
  checked on `/admin/*` only, and opens no project, inbox or chat. An
  agent or runner credential on `/admin/*` is `forbidden`, whatever its
  scopes. It covers the registration settings and the approval or
  rejection of pending accounts (§16.4); no agent ever holds it.
- An account that waits for approval (`account_status: pending`,
  §2.7.5) holds no scope: it is a member of nothing and reaches only its
  own account.
- Cards are readable by every member, so an agent may post a note
  (§6.16) and add a link (§6.13) on any card of its project, whatever
  its role (not as a guest, which posts notes only). It edits a card's fields only as its holder or creator, or
  with `tasks:admin`; it resolves a note only as the card's creator or
  with `tasks:admin`; it never redacts a note or a history entry
  (`events:admin` is a human's). The generated rules (§6.9) tell it not
  to dismiss a human's note without asking that human first.
- Capabilities are per membership and not enforced by the hub (policies,
  not rights, `context/trust.md`): V1 knows `tag` (may tag a release).
  They are shown in the resume packet and in the member view; the forge
  account decides. A capability grants no scope: a one-off right the hub
  enforces is granted by a change of trust or role (`PATCH
  …/members/{id}`) and taken back the same way; a capability records a
  right the hub only shows, such as `tag`.

### 2.4 Presence and leases as side effects

Every authenticated call updates `last_seen_at` on the caller's
membership and, for agents, on the instance and the session. A call by
an instance renews the leases of the claims that instance holds (§6.5),
not those of its team's other instances, with one exception: the events
long-poll (`wait > 0`, §8.3) is presence, not work — a session that only
listens keeps showing `online` while its leases run out, so that a
stuck holder becomes reassignable without anyone guessing. There is no
heartbeat endpoint. A runner's calls update the runner's own
`last_seen_at` and nothing on any membership (§15.3).

### 2.5 Forwarded headers and plain HTTP

TLS is terminated by the operator's reverse proxy or ingress. The hub
takes the scheme and the client address from `X-Forwarded-Proto` and
`X-Forwarded-For` (all header lines joined with `,`, read from the trusted
end; the scheme taken at the same hop as the address) only when the socket
peer is listed in
`MAITY_TRUSTED_PROXIES` (a comma-separated CIDR list; empty by default,
so nothing is trusted and a forwarded header from an arbitrary client
changes nothing). The Helm chart sets it to the ingress; the skeleton's
uvicorn `proxy_headers` default (loopback only) is replaced by this
setting. The bearer-over-TLS rule (§2.2), the join rate limit per source
address (§3.1) and the login limit (§2.1) all read the address and scheme
decided this way.

Without the flag, a login, any cookie-authenticated call, the join
exchange and the runner pairing exchange (§15.2; both responses are a
credential) over plain HTTP from a non-loopback address are
`insecure_transport`, like a bearer credential. The pairing exchange
follows the join exchange in every part of this rule, the flag included. The cookies' `Secure` flag follows the scheme the request
actually arrived with (decided as above), not the flag.

`MAITY_ALLOW_PLAIN_HTTP=1` lets bearer credentials and cookies travel over
plain HTTP from any address, for a hub that is reachable only on a
machine or a private network: the Compose file sets it because it
publishes the port on loopback only, and the hub logs a warning at
startup. A hub that agents reach over a network runs behind TLS and
without the flag.

A join host (§1.1) goes through the same rules: the same trusted proxies,
the same scheme and address decision, `insecure_transport` for the
exchange over plain HTTP. The Helm chart's `ingress.joinHost` adds the
host to the Ingress and its TLS certificate and sets `MAITY_JOIN_URL`;
the routing between the hosts is the hub's (§1.1), so the Ingress sends
the whole host to the hub. A reverse proxy may in addition restrict the
join host at the edge, but only to what §1.1 answers there: `GET` and
`POST` on a single path segment, and `GET` on `/i/` followed by one
segment. A rule that lets one segment through and nothing else breaks
the invitation links.

### 2.6 Human: sign-in without a password

The maintainer's decision of 2026-10-22: besides the password (§2.1),
which stays, a human may sign in with a **device code** approved on a
device that is already signed in, or with a **sign-in link by mail**.
Both end in an ordinary session of §2.1 — the same cookies, lifetime,
CSRF rule and logout — and are for humans only (below and §2.3). The
mail parts rest on the mail settings, verified addresses and signed
links of the notifications contract (#160: §16.2, §18.4, §18.6); until
that is merged, the sign-in link is not offered.

#### 2.6.1 Which methods the login page offers

```
GET /auth/methods
```

Unauthenticated, on the public host only. Answers what the login page
may show; it says nothing about any account:

```json
{ "password": true, "device_code": true, "email_link": true,
  "registration": false, "terms": null }
```

`registration` and `terms` are §2.7.

`password` is always `true`. `device_code` is the instance setting
(§2.6.6). `email_link` is `true` only when the instance setting allows
it **and** the mail settings are complete and enabled (`complete` and
`enabled`, §16.2) — otherwise the login page does not show "Email me a
sign-in link". Whether a given human has a verified address is never
part of the answer.

#### 2.6.2 Device code ("Sign in another device")

The flow, with the signed-in device as **A** (the desktop) and the new
one as **B** (the phone):

1. On A, Profile menu → "Sign in another device": `POST
   /auth/device-codes` (A's cookie session, CSRF) answers a code, a URL
   and the expiry. The dashboard shows the code in three groups of four
   (`K7QM-4XPR-9D2F`), a QR of the URL, and a countdown.
2. On B, the login page → "Have a code?" → the code (or the QR's URL,
   which opens that page with the code filled in): `POST
   /auth/device-login` `{code}`. B shows "Waiting for approval on your
   other device" and a two-digit **match number** (`47`) — not which
   account the code belongs to.
3. A, which waits on `GET /auth/device-codes/{id}?wait=55`, sees the
   code redeemed and shows "Approve this device?" with what the hub
   observed — B's IP address and the time of the redemption — beside
   the browser and operating system B's `User-Agent` claims, and three
   numbers, one of them B's. The human picks the number B shows
   (`POST …/approve` `{number}`) or denies (`POST …/deny`).
4. B, which waits on `GET /auth/device-login?wait=55`, sees `approved`
   — and only now the account: display name, handle, avatar — and calls `POST /auth/device-login/complete`: the hub sets B's own
   session cookies (§2.1). B has a new session; A's session is
   unchanged.

| Endpoint | Caller | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /auth/device-codes` | human (cookie session) | a new code bound to this session and its human; voids an earlier open code of the same session. 201 `{id, code, url, expires_at}` |
| `GET /auth/device-codes/{id}` `?wait=0–55` | the session that created it | `{id, status, expires_at, device?, choices?}`; with `wait`, held until `status` changes, as §8.3. Any other caller, another session of the same human included, gets `not_found` here and on the three calls below |
| `POST /auth/device-codes/{id}/approve` `{number}` | the session that created it | only in `redeemed` (else `conflict`); the number the human picked. Right: 200 with `status: approved`. Wrong: the code is `denied` and the answer is `code_invalid` (number matching, below) |
| `POST /auth/device-codes/{id}/deny` | the session that created it | in `waiting` or `redeemed`; 200 with `status: denied`; the code is dead |
| `DELETE /auth/device-codes/{id}` | the session that created it | cancels; the same as `deny` |
| `POST /auth/device-login` `{code, next?}` | anyone (the new device) | redeems the code; sets the pending cookie (below); 200 `{status: "redeemed", expires_at, match_number}` — no account |
| `GET /auth/device-login` `?wait=0–55` | the browser holding the pending cookie | `{status, expires_at, match_number, account?}`; `account` `{handle, display_name, avatar_url}` only once `status` is `approved` |
| `POST /auth/device-login/complete` | the browser holding the pending cookie | only in `approved` (else `conflict`); sets the session cookies; 200 `{member, next}` (as `POST /auth/login`). Without a pending cookie bound to a code, this and `GET /auth/device-login` are `not_found` |

```json
{ "id": "dvc-3f9a", "status": "redeemed", "expires_at": "2026-10-22T14:05:00Z",
  "device": { "ip": "203.0.113.24", "redeemed_at": "2026-10-22T14:01:12Z",
              "user_agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (iPhone; CPU iPhone OS 19_0 like Mac OS X) …",
              "browser": "Safari", "os": "iOS", "new_device": true },
  "choices": [ 18, 47, 83 ] }
```

- **The code.** 12 characters from Crockford's base32 alphabet
  (`0123456789ABCDEFGHJKMNPQRSTVWXYZ`, 60 bits), drawn from the
  system's secure random source, shown as `XXXX-XXXX-XXXX`. Input is read
  case-insensitively with hyphens and spaces dropped, `I` and `L` read
  as `1`, `O` as `0`. The hub stores `sha256` of the normalised code,
  never the code; the code appears in no response but the one that
  created it.
- **The URL** is `<MAITY_PUBLIC_URL>/sign-in/code#c=K7QM4XPR9D2F`, a
  dashboard path (§16.11) with the code in the fragment, which the
  browser never sends, so it reaches no request log, proxy or
  `Referer`; the hub answers the path with the app shell, and the
  dashboard reads the code from the fragment on that path and removes
  it from the address at once (`history.replaceState`), so it does not
  stay in the browser's history either. The page fills the field in and waits for the human's tap; it does not redeem
  on its own.
- **States.** `waiting` → `redeemed` (B entered it) → `approved` (A said
  yes) → `used` (B completed). `denied` and `expired` end it. A code is
  valid for 5 minutes from its creation; after `approved`, B has 60
  seconds to complete, else the code is `expired`. Whatever the state,
  one code yields at most one session.
- **Single use, first come.** The first `POST /auth/device-login` with
  the code binds it to that browser (the pending cookie); a second one,
  from any browser, is `code_invalid`, the same answer as an unknown,
  expired, denied or used code. When someone else typed a leaked code
  first, A sees *their* device and denies it; the human then creates a
  new code.
- **The approval is the authority.** The code alone grants nothing. Only
  the session that created the code can approve it — not another session
  of the same human, not an agent, not an instance admin — and only
  after a redemption, so the human approves a device they have seen, not
  a code. Revoking or ending A's session (logout, §2.6.5) kills its open
  codes.
- **Bound to the account.** The session B gets belongs to the human who
  created the code, whoever enters it; a code cannot be redeemed into
  another account, and B's request names no account. B learns which
  account it is joining only after A approved, so a guessed or leaked
  code tells its holder nothing about the account behind it.
- **Number matching.** At the redemption the hub draws the match
  number, a value from 10 to 99 from the secure random source, and
  stores it with the code; B shows it. A's dialog shows `choices`:
  three distinct values from 10 to 99 in ascending order, B's number
  and two others drawn the same way. Only the right pick approves; a
  wrong pick denies the code at once, so a second guess needs a new
  code. A human whose own phone shows no number, or a number that is
  not among the three, sees at once that the device in the dialog is
  not theirs — the case of a code read off a shared screen and typed
  first by someone else. The dialog says "Only approve a device you are
  holding now".
- **`device`** is what the hub observed on B's redemption, and the
  dialog leads with it: `ip` as decided by §2.5 and `redeemed_at`, the
  hub's time. `user_agent` (cut at 300 characters, shown as text),
  `browser` and `os` parsed from it (`null` when unknown) are what B's
  browser *claims*; the dialog labels them so ("Says it is Safari on
  iOS") and never shows them alone. `new_device` is `true` when B
  presented no device cookie of this human (§2.6.5); the dialog says
  "First sign-in from this browser" — a hint for the human, not a
  check. V1 shows the IP address and no
  location: an approximate location needs a GeoIP database the operator
  would provide, a later revisit that would add a field then (§1.6).

#### 2.6.3 Sign-in link by mail

Offered when `email_link` is `true` in §2.6.1. On the login page,
"Email me a sign-in link" → an address:

```
POST /auth/email-link   {"address": "maintainer@example.org", "next"?: "/oliver/maity/board"}
```

Unauthenticated. **Always** answers `202 {"expires_in": 900}` and sets
the pending cookie, whether or not the address belongs to anyone: the
hub answers before it looks the address up, and the lookup and the send
run in the background, so neither the body, the status, the cookie nor
the timing tells an address that exists from one that does not. The
rate limits (§2.6.4) count every address alike for the same reason.

A mail is sent only when, at the time of the lookup, the address is a
human's verified address (`address_status: verified`, §18.4; compared
case-insensitively, after trimming), the human's account is not
disabled, the human has not switched sign-in links off for themselves
(below), and the method and the mail settings are still on. While the
instance setting is on but the mail settings are incomplete or
`enabled: false`, the call still answers `202` and sends nothing — the
same answer as everywhere else in this flow (`GET /auth/methods`
already tells the login page not to offer it). A new request voids the
earlier unused link and code requested from the **same source
address** for that human; a request from another source address leaves
them alone, so nobody elsewhere can void the link the human is about to
use.

**The human's own switch.** Besides the instance setting (§2.6.6), each
human may turn sign-in links off for their account: `email.sign_in_link`
in the notification settings (#160, §18.4), `true` by default,
`PATCH /me/notification-settings` `{"email": {"sign_in_link": false}}`.
With `false` the hub sends no link and no code to that human —
`POST /auth/email-link` still answers `202` as for any address, and
`GET /auth/methods` is unchanged, since it never speaks about an
account. Turning it off voids an open link and code. The dashboard
shows the switch with the sentence "Turn this off if an agent or anyone
else can read this mailbox: whoever reads it can sign in as you"
(§2.3).

**Changing the verified address.** The verified address is a sign-in
factor, so changing or removing it (`email.address` in #160, §18.4)
needs the human's own confirmation in a form that neither a mailbox nor
a moment at an unlocked dashboard provides. How a session was made or
how young it is does not count: a device-code session can be approved
on an unlocked dashboard, and a mail-link session is fresh by
definition.

- **A human with a password** enters it in the same request:
  `current_password` beside `email` in the `PATCH` (#160, §18.4).
  Missing: `invalid` with `details.fields.current_password: "required"`;
  wrong: `invalid` with `details.fields.current_password: "mismatch"`,
  counted against the login limit of §2.1 as a wrong `current` of
  `POST /auth/password` is. Right: the change goes on as #160 §18.4
  describes (the new address is verified by its link).
- **A human without a password** (an account that has never set one)
  needs the change approved from a session of theirs that is **at
  least 24 hours old**. A `PATCH` from such a session is that approval
  and goes on at once. From a younger session the change is held:
  `202` with `email.address_change: {id, address, requested_at,
  session_id}` — `id` an immutable `adc-<random>` of this one change,
  the address `null` for a removal — shown with "Approve" and "Reject"
  in every session of the human that may act on it. Both calls name
  what they act on and need a session **in good standing** (§2.6.5):
  `POST /me/notification-settings/email/address-change/approve` `{id,
  address}` from a session in good standing that is at least 24 hours
  old lets it go on (younger: `forbidden` with `details.reason:
  session_too_new`); `POST …/address-change/reject` `{id, address}` from
  a session in good standing drops it. A session not in good standing
  can neither approve nor reject a held change, nor replace it with a
  `PATCH` of its own: each is `forbidden` with `details.reason:
  not_in_good_standing`; it may file a change only while none is held.
  A `PATCH` that is itself the approval (from a session at least 24
  hours old) also needs good standing. A held change exists once per
  human: a newer `PATCH` of the address from a session in good standing
  replaces it atomically with a new `id`, and an approval or
  rejection naming the old `id`, or an `address` that is not the held
  change's, is `conflict` (§1.3) and changes nothing — so a session
  that showed address A can never approve an address B that a younger
  session put in its place. A held change lapses after 7 days. A human
  with no session that old waits until one is.

The old address is notified as before: when the new address is
confirmed, or the address is removed, the **old** address
gets a `security` mail ("The sign-in address of your Maity account was
changed to m…@example.net at <time> from <browser> on <os>, <ip>; if
this was not you, sign in and end your other sessions"), with the new
address masked to its first character and its domain. This mail is
sent even though the old address no longer receives notifications, and
whatever `email.kinds.security.mode` says: `off` silences the alerts of
new sign-ins, never this notice. The change also writes the account
record `email_address_changed` (below), which is a `security`
notification in the dashboard.
**The mail.** Plain text in the human's `language` (§18.4), with the
rules of §18.5 for headers and content, minus the unsubscribe parts: a
sign-in mail is a reply to a request, not a notification, so it ignores
the human's notification modes, quiet hours and the per-human hourly
cap. Because anyone can ask for one without signing in, sign-in mails
have **limits of their own**: per source address (§2.6.4) and an
instance-wide cap, `sign_in_max_per_hour` (#160 §16.2, default 60);
over either, the request answers `202` as always and nothing is sent.
Sign-in mails never count against the budget for security mails or the
one for notifications, so no number of anonymous requests can delay an
alert, a verification or the old-address notice — those are queued,
never dropped (#160 §16.2). Subject `[Maity] Sign-in
link`. Body:

- the link `<MAITY_PUBLIC_URL>/mail/sign-in/{token}`, valid 15 minutes;
- "Or enter this code in the browser where you asked for it:
  `482 913`" — six digits;
- when and from which browser, operating system and address the request
  came;
- "If you did not ask for this, ignore this mail; nothing happens
  without the link or the code." Nothing else: no handle beyond the
  greeting's display name, no project, no other link.

**The link page.** `/mail/sign-in/{token}` is outside the API, on the
public host only (a join host answers it with its `302`, §1.1), with the
rules of §18.6: the request log masks the token as `…`, an invalid,
expired or used token is the page that says the link no longer works
(status `not_found`, never which reason).

| Method | Effect |
|---|---|
| `GET` | a page "Sign in to Maity as <display name> (<handle>)" with one button "Sign in on this device"; changes nothing, sets nothing but the form cookie below. Mail scanners and link previews open it harmlessly |
| `POST` | signs in **this** browser: a fresh session (§2.1), then `303` to the stored `next` (§2.6.5) or `/` |

The token follows §18.6: the base64url of `{human id, purpose:
"sign_in", nonce, expiry}` and an HMAC-SHA-256 over it with
`MAITY_MAIL_SIGNING_KEY`, so a forged token is refused before any
lookup. Single use needs state, so the hub also stores `sha256(nonce)`
with the expiry; using the link or the code marks both used. The
`POST` must carry the form field the `GET` page put next to a
`maity_form` cookie (`HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict;
Path=/mail/sign-in`, 10 minutes, a random value; the field must match
it), and a `Sec-Fetch-Site` that is absent or other than `same-origin`
is refused, so no
other site can submit it for a visitor.

**The code.** For when the mail is read on another device than the one
that asked:

```
POST /auth/email-code   {"code": "482913"}
```

Valid only in the browser that made the request — the one holding the
pending cookie of that `POST /auth/email-link` — and only for that
request's human; it carries no address. Spaces are ignored. A wrong
code is `code_invalid`; the fifth wrong code voids the code (the link
stays valid). The 20th wrong mailed code for one human in a day, from
any source, voids **every** outstanding mailed code of that human at
once (their links stay valid), and until the day ends mails to that
human carry the link only and no code: the six digits are the only
guessable part, and the link — signed and 15 minutes long — is not. So
a guess spread over many source addresses, each holding a live code of
its own, gets at most 20 tries per human per day. Right: a fresh session as `POST /auth/login`, 200
`{member, next}`; the link is then used too. The code is stored as an
HMAC with the signing key, never in clear.

#### 2.6.4 Rate limits and abuse

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| `POST /auth/device-codes` | 5 per 10 minutes per human |
| `POST /auth/device-login` | 10 per minute per source address, every attempt; and 60 wrong codes per minute across the instance — past that, every redemption is `rate_limited` for a minute (a distributed guess at 60 bits cannot get far; the password still works). This breaker is a known denial of service: a few source addresses can keep device-code sign-in off for the whole instance. It is accepted on purpose — a per-source limit alone would let a distributed guess run — and must not be "fixed" into one |
| `POST /auth/email-link` | 3 per 15 minutes and 10 per day per (address, source address), existing or not; 10 per hour per source address; sign-in mails sent across the instance at most `sign_in_max_per_hour` (#160 §16.2, default 60) — a budget of their own, apart from security and notification mail |
| `POST /auth/email-code` | 5 wrong codes per mailed code; 20 wrong codes per human per day, after which every outstanding code of that human is void (§2.6.3); 10 per minute per source address, shared with the login limit of §2.1 |
| Long-polls on `GET /auth/device-codes/{id}` and `GET /auth/device-login` | one per session or pending cookie; a second supersedes the first |

Over a limit: `rate_limited` with `Retry-After` (§1.3). For
`POST /auth/email-link` the per-address limit and the instance cap are
applied as `202` with nothing sent, like an unknown address — a `429`
there would tell an address that is being used from one that is not;
only the per-source-address limit answers `429`. A caller who spends
the instance cap delays nobody's alert: it stops sign-in mails for the
rest of the hour, nothing else, and the device code and the password
are unaffected.

**No lock-out through the limits.** The per-address limit counts per
(address, source address), so requests from elsewhere do not spend the
budget of the human's own network: someone who knows the address can
fill the mailbox with sign-in mails (at most 10 per day per source
address they control) but cannot spend the human's per-address budget
nor void the human's link (§2.6.3). Whoever controls enough source
addresses can spend the instance cap and stop sign-in mails for
everyone until the hour ends — the same accepted kind of denial as the
device-code breaker above, limited to the mail link. The device code, the legitimate path
for a human who is signed in anywhere, has no per-address limit at all
and is never affected by mail limits; the password is not either.

#### 2.6.5 Rules every method keeps

- **Session fixation.** Every method issues a fresh session id and a
  fresh CSRF token at the moment it completes, never earlier, and never
  takes over an id the browser presented. A browser that already holds
  a session (of any human) has that session ended first. The pending
  cookie and the form cookie are cleared on completion and never
  authenticate anything but their own flow.
- **The pending cookie.** `maity_pending`: `HttpOnly; Secure;
  SameSite=Strict; Path=/api/v1/auth`, a random value of 32 bytes
  (stored as `sha256`), lifetime that of its flow (5 minutes for a
  device code, 15 for a mail). One per browser; a new flow replaces it.
  It is the only thing that lets B collect the session in §2.6.2 and
  the only thing that makes a mailed code usable in §2.6.3.
- **CSRF before a session exists.** `POST /auth/device-login`, `…/complete`,
  `/auth/email-link` and `/auth/email-code` refuse a `Sec-Fetch-Site`
  of `cross-site` or `same-site` (`forbidden`), like a login (§2.1), and
  the pending cookie is `SameSite=Strict`; so no other site can start
  or finish a sign-in in a visitor's browser. Calls made with a session
  (`/auth/device-codes/*`, `/auth/sessions/*`) carry `X-CSRF-Token` as
  every cookie call. What stays: a human who opens someone else's link
  and presses the button is signed in to that person's account — the
  page names the account in its heading for that reason.
- **`next`.** The login page passes its `next` to `POST /auth/login`,
  `POST /auth/device-login` and `POST /auth/email-link`; the hub
  stores it with the flow (never in a mail or a URL it sends) and
  answers it back after checking. Allowed is only a dashboard path on
  the public host (§16.11): a path on this host that starts with `/`, at
  most 512 characters, without a backslash, a control or whitespace
  character, a `#`, or `//`, whose first segment is not a hub path
  (§16.11: not `/api/…`, `/assets/…`, `/mail/…` and the others there).
  Anything else is replaced by `/` silently. The hub never redirects to
  a host, a scheme or a path outside the dashboard.
- **Transport.** Every endpoint here follows §2.5: over plain HTTP from
  a non-loopback address without `MAITY_ALLOW_PLAIN_HTTP` it is
  `insecure_transport`. On a join host none of them exists (§1.1).
- **Disabled.** When an instance setting turns a method off (§2.6.6),
  its open codes and links are void at once and its endpoints answer
  `forbidden` with `details.reason: method_disabled`; sessions already
  made stay.
- **Ended with the password.** `POST /auth/password` ends every other
  session of the human, however it was made, and voids their open codes
  and links.

**The session list.** Profile → Sessions:

| Endpoint | Caller | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /auth/sessions` `?ended=true` | human | the caller's own sessions, newest first; with `ended=true` also the ones ended in the last 30 days |
| `DELETE /auth/sessions/{id}` | human | ends one of the caller's own sessions, and every session it approved by device code that the caller may end (below); the current one is a logout; idempotent; answers the session as it is now, with `skipped` naming the approved sessions it did not end |
| `POST /auth/sessions/end-others` | human | ends every session of the caller but the current one; answers the list of live sessions |

**Good standing.** A session is **in good standing** when it was
signed in by password, or when its own `session_created` item has been
marked read by an allowed session through `ids` (below) — never by
`up_to`, by age or by the record's expiry. The session list shows it
(`good_standing`). Good standing is what lets a session end others,
mark sign-in alerts read and act on a held address change (§2.6.3).

**Who may end which session.**

- A session **in good standing** may end any session of the human, at
  any age, newer ones included — through `DELETE /auth/sessions/{id}`,
  `end-others` or the banner's "End this session".
- A session **not in good standing** never ends a session that is in
  good standing (`forbidden`, `details.reason: not_in_good_standing`;
  `end-others` from it ends only the other sessions not in good
  standing). While it is younger than 1 hour it ends no session older
  than itself either (`forbidden`, `details.reason: session_too_new`).
  It may always end itself (a logout).

So a session obtained through a mailbox or a stolen device code cannot
end the sessions that show the alert of its sign-in, at any age, and a
human who signs in again with the password gets a session in good
standing that ends it at once. A password change (§2.1) still ends
every other session, since it needs the password.

```json
{ "items": [
  { "id": "hss-41c0", "current": true, "method": "password",
    "created_at": "2026-10-22T08:02:11Z", "last_seen_at": "2026-10-22T14:01:30Z",
    "expires_at": "2026-11-05T14:01:30Z", "browser": "Firefox", "os": "Linux",
    "ip": "198.51.100.7", "approved_by": null, "good_standing": true },
  { "id": "hss-41c7", "current": false, "method": "device_code",
    "created_at": "2026-10-22T14:01:40Z", "last_seen_at": "2026-10-22T14:01:40Z",
    "expires_at": "2026-11-05T14:01:40Z", "browser": "Safari", "os": "iOS",
    "ip": "203.0.113.24", "approved_by": "hss-41c0", "good_standing": false,
    "created": { "record": "acr-118", "ip": "203.0.113.24", "browser": "Safari", "os": "iOS" },
    "ended_at": null, "ended_by": null } ] }
```

`id` is a public id, never the cookie's value. `method` is `password`,
`device_code`, `email_link`, `email_code` or `register` (the session a
completed registration starts, §2.7.1); `second_factor` says whether
the sign-in included the second factor (§2.8.2). `approved_by` names the
session that approved a device code. `ip` is the one of the latest
call; `created` is the account record of the sign-in (below), with the
address and browser the session started from. `ended_at` and
`ended_by` (`logout`, `revoked`, `end_others`, `expired`,
`password_change`, `second_factor_disabled`, `second_factor_reset`,
§2.8) are set on an ended session; an ended session shows no `ip`, and
the hub keeps none for it. A session of another
human is `not_found`. `GET /auth/session` (§2.1) gains `session_id`,
the current session's `id`.

**The device cookie.** At every completed sign-in the hub sets
`maity_device` (`HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/`, a random
32-byte value stored as `sha256` with the human, 400 days, kept on
logout) unless the browser already holds one of this human; a browser
shared by two humans holds one value per human. It authenticates
nothing and has one use only: the device-code approval dialog (§2.6.2)
says "This browser has signed in to your account before" or "First
sign-in from this browser" (`device.new_device`). It decides nothing
about alerts: every mail sign-in is alerted, whatever cookie the
browser presents (below).

**Telling the human.** Every new session, whichever the method, writes
`session_created` `{session_id, method, browser, os, ip, approved_by}`
as an **account record**: an audit record of the human's account, not
an event — it belongs to no project, so §8 does not carry it and no
project member, owner, admin, instance admin or agent reads it.
Account records are the second source of notifications beside events
(#160, §18.1): ids `acr-<n>` from a sequence of their own, never the
event sequence, so they leave no gap in any project's `/events` from
which the sign-ins of humans could be timed; kept 90 days, readable by
the human alone. The record is shown with its session in Profile →
Sessions (`created` above), and ending a session writes
`session_ended` there in the same way. `session_created` becomes a
notification of the kind `security` (#160, §18.1), title `New sign-in:
<browser> on <os> (<method>)`, linking to Profile → Sessions.

- **In the dashboard** the `security` notification is always there: it
  has no browser or mail switch that hides it from the bell, and it
  counts in `counts.security` (not in `total`).
- **Who may mark it read.** A `session_created` item is marked read
  only from a session that **existed before** the sign-in it reports —
  never from the session it reports on, and never from any session
  created after it — and only when that earlier session is itself in
  good standing (above). It is marked read only through `ids` — the
  explicit "This was me", or the item in the session list — and never
  through `up_to`: "mark all read" skips every `security` item, so
  tidying the bell never confirms a sign-in. A `POST
  /me/notifications/read` from a session that may not mark the item
  skips it as well, and marks the rest. So a session obtained through a mailbox can hide
  neither its own alert nor that of a second session it obtains next
  (by another mail sign-in, or by a device code it approves). An item
  that no session may mark read — the human had no session in good
  standing at the time — stays listed and unread in the bell until its
  record expires (90 days). Security items are exempt from the 30-day
  rule of #160 §18.2 that counts older items as read: they stay listed
  and unread until an allowed session marks them read or the record
  expires. Only that marking grants good standing; age, expiry or any
  other automatic reading never does — a session whose own item
  expired unread stays out of good standing.
- **Every mail sign-in is an alert** — method `email_link` or
  `email_code`, whatever device cookie the browser presented. It is
  shown in **every other session** of the human at once, not only in
  the bell: each open dashboard long-polls the notifications (#160,
  §18.2) and shows a banner "New sign-in by mail: <browser> on <os>,
  <ip>, <time>" with **End this session** (`DELETE
  /auth/sessions/{id}`, one click, no confirmation dialog; it also ends
  every session the reported one approved by device code, and those
  approved by them in turn) and, in a session that may mark the item
  read (above), **This was me**. The banner stays while the item is
  unread and the reported session, or a session it approved, is still
  active; a dashboard opened later shows it too. The item carries the
  new session's id (`target: {type: "session", id}`); the session it
  reports on shows no banner. So a mail sign-in that an agent with
  mailbox access made cannot be hidden by deleting a mail, from the
  session it obtained, or from a session it obtains next (§2.3); and
  that session, not being in good standing, cannot end the human's
  sessions in good standing that show the banner, at any age (above).
- **By mail** it goes to the human's verified address, `immediate` by
  default; `email.kinds.security.mode` (#160, §18.4) is `immediate` or
  `off` — no digest, since a delayed alert is no alert — and quiet
  hours do not hold it. The mail carries the time, method, browser,
  operating system and IP address of the new session and the link to
  Profile → Sessions, with the unsubscribe line for its kind (§18.5);
  never a session id, a code or a link that signs anyone in. A human
  without a verified address, or an instance without mail, gets the
  dashboard notification only. The mail counts against the security
  budget (`security_max_per_hour`, #160 §16.2), not against the
  notification budget or the sign-in mail cap; over the budget it is
  queued for the next hour, never dropped.

`session_ended` is not notified.

**Agents and runners.** None of this is for them: an agent or runner
credential on any endpoint of this section is `forbidden` with
`details.reason: humans_only` (§2.1, §2.3), and no call with such a
credential creates, redeems, approves or completes a code, asks for a
link or uses one, or lists or ends a human's sessions. What the hub
cannot do is tell an agent that calls these endpoints *without* its
credential from a browser; for the sign-in link that means an agent
holding the human's mailbox can sign in as the human, and §2.3 states
that limit and what the hub does about it.

#### 2.6.6 Instance settings

```
GET, PATCH /admin/settings/sign-in
```

Scope `instance:admin`, human only (§16.1). Each value may come from the
environment or from the instance admin, with the source rules of §16.2:
the environment wins and a `PATCH` of a value it sets is `invalid` with
`set_by_environment`.

| Environment | Field | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MAITY_SIGN_IN_DEVICE_CODE` | `device_code` | `true` | device codes (§2.6.2) |
| `MAITY_SIGN_IN_EMAIL_LINK` | `email_link` | `true` | sign-in links and codes by mail (§2.6.3); offered only while the mail settings are complete and enabled, and sent only to a verified address whose human has not switched it off |
| `MAITY_SIGN_IN_SECOND_FACTOR` | `second_factor` | `optional` | `off`, `optional` or `required_admins` (§2.8.5); available only with `MAITY_SECRET_KEY` (`missing: ["secret_key"]`) |

```json
{ "password": { "value": true, "source": "fixed" },
  "device_code": { "value": true, "source": "default" },
  "email_link": { "value": true, "source": "admin" },
  "email_link_available": false, "missing": ["mail"] }
```

`password` cannot be turned off (a `PATCH` of it is `invalid` with
`fixed`). `email_link_available` says whether the login page offers it
right now, `missing` why not: `switched_off` (the setting is `false`),
`mail` (the mail settings are not complete and enabled), and
`not_implemented` while the hub does not serve the sign-in link yet. A change is not an
event; the accounts design's instance audit log records it (pending).

#### 2.6.7 The dashboard's part

- **Login page.** The password form as today; below it "Have a code?"
  when `device_code` is on, and "Email me a sign-in link" when
  `email_link` is on (§2.6.1). After the mail request: "If this address
  belongs to an account, a link is on its way", with a field for the
  six-digit code. After a device code: "Waiting for approval on your
  other device"; after the approval, the account (avatar, name, handle)
  and then signed in.
- **Profile menu → Sign in another device.** The code, its QR (made in
  the dashboard's own code, no third-party script, §1.1), a countdown,
  and then the approval dialog: first what the hub observed (IP
  address, time), then the browser and operating system the device
  claims, labelled as claimed; "Only approve a device you are holding
  now"; the three numbers to pick from, and "Deny" — "Deny" is the
  default button, and there is no plain "Approve".
- **Profile → Sessions.** The list of §2.6.5 with "End" per session,
  "End all other sessions", and the ended sessions of the last 30 days.
- **The mail sign-in banner** of §2.6.5 in every other open session,
  with "This was me" only where that session may mark it read.
- **Notification settings** (#160, §18.8) gain the `security` mail switch
  and "Allow sign-in links by mail" (`email.sign_in_link`), with the
  mailbox warning of §2.6.3.
- **Changing the address** asks for the password in the same form; for
  a human without one it says the change waits for approval from a
  session at least 24 hours old, and such sessions show the held change
  with "Approve" and "Reject" (§2.6.3).
- **Ending sessions** from a session not in good standing: "End" on a
  session in good standing is disabled, with "Confirm this session's
  sign-in from another session first"; and, while it is younger than
  1 hour, "End" on an
  older session and "End all other sessions" are disabled, with "This
  session is too new to end older ones" (§2.6.5).

### 2.7 Human: registration

The maintainer's direction of 2026-10-23 (`context/scope.md`, "One
codebase, three ways to run it"): an instance runs alone at home, as a
team's own instance, or as an open hosted one, and the three differ
only in settings. This section is how a person gets an account on their
own; the settings that decide whether they may are the instance admin's
(§16.4). Plans and their limits are part two of this contract, a
separate change: until it exists, a registered account has exactly the
limits every account has today, and the account's plan is the
operator's default plan once part two defines one.

**Modes.** The instance setting `registration` (§16.4):

| Mode | Who may register |
|---|---|
| `closed` (default) | nobody, except an address that an open address-bound invitation admits (§3.4). Accounts come only from the operator — the first admin, `maity-hub owner create` (§2.1, §16) — and, once they exist, from invitations (§3.4) and joins (§3, agents). With mail available the endpoints answer `202` like the other modes and drop every non-admitted address in the background (§2.7.1); without mail they answer `forbidden` with `details.reason: registration_closed` before reading the body |
| `allowlist` | a person whose address matches a listed domain or a listed exact address (below) |
| `open` | anyone with an address that can be verified |

A fresh instance is `closed`; no migration, chart value or command
opens it, only the instance admin's setting or the operator's
environment. `allowlist` and `open` need mail: without complete and
enabled mail settings (§16.2) the switch is refused (`mail_required`,
§16.4), and when mail stops being complete or enabled later, the
instance registers nobody until it is again (below). A mode never
narrows invitations or joins: they are the project's way in, and
registration is the instance's.

**The allowlist.** Two lists, `domains` and `addresses` (§16.4). A
domain entry is written `@example.com` and matches an address whose
domain is exactly that domain, compared case-insensitively — not its
subdomains: `@sub.example.com` is its own entry. An address entry
matches that exact address, compared as §2.6.3 compares (trimmed, case
ignored). Both follow the address syntax of §18.4. An address matches
when either list matches.

**What the login page learns.** `GET /auth/methods` (§2.6.1) gains
`registration`: `true` while the mode is `allowlist` or `open` and mail
is complete and enabled, else `false` — also `false` under `allowlist`
while both lists are empty, since nobody could register then (the admin
sees it as `missing: ["allowlist"]`, §16.4); and `terms`: `{url, version}` or
`null` (§16.4). It says nothing about the lists' entries or any account;
only whether an allowlist has any entry follows from `registration`. The
login page shows "Create an account" only with `registration: true`.

#### 2.7.1 The flow: the address is verified before an account exists

```
POST /auth/register   {"address": "ada@example.com", "password": "…", "next"?: "/"}
```

Unauthenticated, on the public host only, with the rules of §2.6.5 for
transport, `Sec-Fetch-Site` and `next`.

1. **Synchronous checks, none of which looks at an account.** Mail is
   incomplete or disabled: `forbidden` with `details.reason:
   registration_closed`, before the body is read. With mail, every
   mode — `closed` included — reads the body: `address` follows §18.4,
   `password` §2.1 (at least 12 characters) — `invalid` otherwise, with
   `details.fields`. Then the per-source limit (§2.7.3). Under `closed`
   the hub answers the same `202` as under the other modes and drops
   the request in the background unless an invitation admits the
   address (§3.4): the mode never shows in the synchronous answer, so
   an invited address is not told apart from any other.
2. **The answer.** `202 {"expires_in": 86400}`, always, from here on. The
   hub hashes the password (scrypt, §2.1) for every request before it
   answers, so every accepted request costs the same; the lookup, the
   allowlist check and the send run in the background, as in §2.6.3.
   Neither the body, the status nor the timing tells an address that
   has an account from one that has none, nor a listed address from an
   unlisted one.
3. **In the background**, at the time of the lookup:
   - The address is not admitted: under `allowlist` not listed, under
     `closed` always — unless an open, address-bound invitation admits
     it (§3.4: the invitation is open, its project is not closed and
     its issuer still holds the authority it needs, the same predicate
     accept uses). Not admitted: no mail, and the request is dropped.
   - The address is the verified address of an account (§18.4), or of a
     rejected registration that is still blocked (§16.4): one mail,
     "Someone asked to create a Maity account with this address on
     <public URL>. You have one already: sign in at <login page>. If
     this was not you, ignore this mail." No link that creates or signs
     in anything, no handle. A blocked address gets no mail.
   - Otherwise: a **pending registration** — the address, the password
     hash, the source address, the terms version shown (§2.7.2), the
     stored `next`, created and expiry time (24 hours) — and one mail
     with a signed link.
   Both mails count against the registration budget (§16.2); over it,
   nothing is sent, as for sign-in mails. Only the mail differs.
4. **The mail.** Plain text in the language the request's
   `Accept-Language` names, where the hub has it, else English; rules of
   §18.5 for headers, no unsubscribe part (a reply to a request).
   Subject `[Maity] Confirm your address`. The link
   `<MAITY_PUBLIC_URL>/mail/register/{token}`, valid 24 hours; when and
   from which browser, operating system and address the request came;
   "If you did not ask for this, ignore this mail; no account is
   created without the link and the password chosen with it." Nothing
   else: no handle, no project, no other link.
5. **The link page.** `/mail/register/{token}` follows §2.6.3's link page
   and §18.6: outside the API, public host only, token masked in the
   request log, a `GET` that changes nothing and sets only the form
   cookie (`maity_form`, `Path=/mail/register`), a `POST` that needs the
   form field and refuses a `Sec-Fetch-Site` other than `same-origin`.
   The `GET` shows "Create your Maity account for <address>" with four
   fields: the **password chosen at registration**, the **handle**, the
   **display name**, and — when the instance has terms — "I accept the
   terms (<url>, version <version>)", unchecked, for the instance's
   current version. The form carries that version in a hidden field the
   hub signs together with the registration token (HMAC under
   `MAITY_MAIL_SIGNING_KEY` over `{token nonce, terms version}`), so the
   `POST` says exactly which version the person saw (§2.7.2). Under the
   form the page links the legal pages the instance serves (§16.7.1:
   imprint, privacy notice, terms of use), as the dashboard's
   registration form does.
6. **Completion** (`POST` of that page). In this order: the admission is
   checked again, atomically with the completion (the mode changed, the
   address no longer listed, or the admitting invitation no longer
   admits — revoked, expired, used, voided, its project closed or its
   issuer without authority: the page says registration is closed,
   nothing is created and the pending registration is void); the password must match the stored hash (a
   wrong one is the page's error; the fifth voids the pending
   registration); the handle and the display name follow §2.7.4; the
   terms box must be checked when terms are set, and the signed version
   in the form must be the instance's current one — if the terms changed
   since the page was shown, nothing is created and no acceptance is
   recorded, and the page comes back with the current terms, unchecked,
   asking to confirm them anew (§2.7.2). The hub then claims the
   address (below) and, in the same transaction, creates the human
   account with the address as its verified address (`address_status:
   verified`, §18.4), the terms acceptance (§2.7.2) and `account_status`
   `active` or `pending` (approval, §2.7.5); voids every other pending
   registration of the address; signs this browser in with a fresh
   session (§2.1, §2.6.5; `method: "register"` in the session list); and
   answers `303` to the stored `next`, or, for a pending account, to the
   pending page.

**One address, one account: the claim at completion.** A verified
address belongs to at most one account (the uniqueness rule of §18.4).
The hub enforces it with a unique constraint on the accounts'
normalized verified address — trimmed and lower-cased, the comparison
§2.6.3 uses — and takes the claim under a per-address lock that the
address verification and the address change of §18.4 take as well.
So of any number of completions and verifications racing for one
address, exactly one wins: it writes the address, and in the same
transaction every other pending registration of that address becomes
unusable. A loser — a completion whose address is now verified on an
account, its own pending registration voided, or the constraint
refusing its insert — creates nothing, authenticates nobody, never
signs in to the winning account or any existing one, and sees the same
page as an expired link: "This link can no longer be used"
(`not_found`), never why. The lookup in step 3 is a filter that spares
a mail, not the guard; the claim is the guard.

The token follows §18.6: the base64url of `{pending registration id,
purpose: "register", nonce, expiry}` with an HMAC-SHA-256 over it under
`MAITY_MAIL_SIGNING_KEY`, a forged token refused before any lookup;
single use, by `sha256(nonce)` stored with the pending registration. An
invalid, expired, used or voided token is the page that says the link
no longer works (`not_found`, never which). A new request for the same
address from the same source address voids the earlier unused one; one
from another source address leaves it alone (as §2.6.3). At most 5
pending registrations exist per address; a sixth voids the oldest.
Pending registrations are deleted at expiry: an unverified address and
its password hash are kept at most 24 hours.

**Why the password is asked again.** The link proves the mailbox, the
password proves the person who asked. Someone who registers another
person's address cannot complete without that mailbox, and the owner of
the mailbox who follows a link they did not ask for cannot complete
into a password someone else chose. The link works on any device, so
reading the mail on a phone is enough.

**Agents.** An agent or runner credential on `/auth/register` or
`/mail/register/*` is `forbidden` with `details.reason: humans_only`
(§2.3). Called without a credential, the endpoint cannot tell an agent
from a browser — the limit §2.3 states for the sign-in link: an agent
that controls a mailbox can register an account for that address on an
`open` or matching `allowlist` instance. That is a new account, never
access to an existing human's, and `approval: operator` (§2.7.5) is the
operator's answer where it matters.

**OAuth** (registering with a forge or another identity provider) is a
later change of its own; it will keep the modes, the allowlist on the
provider's verified address, approval and terms of this section.

#### 2.7.2 Terms

When the instance sets terms (`terms: {url, version}`, §16.4), the
completion page requires their acceptance, and the account records
`terms: {version, accepted_at}`, the hub's time. What is accepted is the
version the person saw: the link page shows the instance's current
version and the form carries it, signed by the hub with the
registration token (§2.7.1). When the instance's version changed between
the page and its `POST`, the `POST` creates no account and records no
acceptance; the page shows the current terms again, unchecked, and asks
for a fresh confirmation. The version stored with the pending
registration is only what the request saw and is never recorded as
accepted. Accounts made otherwise — the operator's, invitations — record nothing.
What a change of version does to existing accounts — whether they
must accept again — is a separate question and not part of this
contract. `GET /me` carries `member.terms` (§5.1) for a human.

#### 2.7.3 Rate limits and abuse

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| `POST /auth/register` per source address | 10 per hour; `rate_limited` (`429`) — the one limit that answers `429`, since it speaks only about the caller |
| per (address, source address) | 3 per 15 minutes, 10 per day, existing account or not; over it `202` and nothing is sent |
| per address, all sources | 20 per day; over it `202` and nothing is sent, so the instance cannot be used to fill a stranger's mailbox |
| instance breaker | more than `MAITY_REGISTRATION_BREAKER` requests (default 120) per minute across the instance, every request counted: every `POST /auth/register` is `rate_limited` for a minute |
| registration mails | `registration_max_per_hour` (§16.2, default 30), a budget of their own; over it `202` and nothing is sent |
| completion | 5 wrong passwords per pending registration (then void); 10 completion attempts per minute per source address, shared with the login limit of §2.1 |
| new accounts | `max_new_accounts_per_hour` (§16.4, default 20) across the instance; over it the completion page says to try again later and keeps the pending registration |

The breaker is the same accepted denial as the device-code breaker
(§2.6.4): a few source addresses can stop registration for everyone for
a minute at a time, and that is preferred to a per-source limit alone,
which a distributed flood would pass. It never touches sign-in, mail
of any other kind, or existing accounts. Someone who knows an address
can spend its per-address day (20 requests) and delay that person's
registration to the next day; nothing more.

#### 2.7.4 Handle and display name

A human's handle follows the agent profiles' syntax
(`[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{1,30}`, §6.3) and is unique among human accounts
and organisations, their aliases included (§6.24, §6.26), since the
login takes it (§2.1) and a project's owner is named by it (§6.25);
compared as written, it is lower case by the syntax. It is never a
reserved first segment (§16.11): `invalid`, `details.fields.handle:
"reserved"`. `display_name` is 1–64 characters, no control
character. A taken handle is the completion page's error "This handle is
taken" — shown only to someone who proved the mailbox and the
password, and counted in the completion limit (§2.7.3). The human
renames it later themselves; the old handle stays theirs as an alias
(§6.24).

#### 2.7.5 Approval

With `approval: operator` (§16.4), a completed registration makes an
account with `account_status: pending`. Its sessions are **restricted
pending sessions**: real sessions that hold no scope and see only their
own pending status.

- **Getting one.** The session the completion starts (§2.7.1); later,
  `POST /auth/login` with the handle and the password (§2.1); and, where
  the instance offers it, a sign-in link by mail (§2.6.3). Each gives
  the same restricted session. Device codes cannot be used: creating or
  approving one needs a session in good standing, and a pending session
  is never in good standing, however it was made (an exception to
  §2.6.5's password rule) — `POST /auth/device-codes` and its approval
  are `forbidden` with `details.reason: account_pending`.
- **What it may do.** `GET /me` answers `member` with `account_status:
  "pending"` and `projects: []`; `GET /auth/session`; `POST
  /auth/logout`; its own sessions (`GET /auth/sessions`, `DELETE
  /auth/sessions/{id}`, `POST /auth/sessions/end-others`, under the
  rules §2.6.5 sets for sessions not in good standing); `POST
  /auth/password`. `GET /auth/methods` stays what it is for everyone:
  it never depends on an account.
- **Everything else** is `forbidden` with `details.reason:
  account_pending`, before any side effect: no project, no agent
  profile, no notification, no address change, no search. The dashboard
  shows one page: "Your account waits for the operator's approval."
- A pending account is a member of nothing and nobody can make it one
  until it is approved. On approval its sessions stay and gain what
  every human session has, good standing included by §2.6.5's rules
  from then on.

The instance admin approves or rejects it (§16.4). On approval it is
`active`, the person gets a mail "Your Maity account is approved" with
the login page's link (security budget, §16.2) and the account record
`registration_approved`, which is no notification (§18.1): the mail and
the next sign-in tell the person. On rejection
the account is deleted with its sessions, the person gets a mail with
the reason (security budget), and the address is blocked from
registering for 30 days (§16.4). A pending account that nobody decides
on is deleted after 30 days, with the same block and a mail without
reason ("was not approved in time"). With `approval: automatic` the
account is `active` at once.

#### 2.7.6 Privacy

A registered person sees their own account and the projects they are a
member of, and nothing else of the instance: `GET /projects` lists the
caller's memberships only (§6.1), `GET /agents` the caller's own
profiles (§6.3), the `@` list and the member view are a project's
(§6.2, §8.6), and no endpoint searches, lists or resolves accounts
outside a shared project. The one list of accounts is the instance
admin's (§16.1, §16.4). Registration adds no read: an open instance is
as private between its accounts as a team's own. Avatars keep the read
rule of §6.10: an account that shares no project with their owner does
not read them, the instance admin aside.

### 2.8 Human: two-factor sign-in

A human may add a **second factor**: a time-based code
from an authenticator app (TOTP, RFC 6238), with ten **recovery codes**
for when the app is lost. Once enrolled, every new session of the human
asks for it, whichever first factor started the session, and a few
sensitive calls ask for it again (**step-up**, §2.8.4). Agents and
runners are not affected: they sign every request with a credential of
their own (§2.2) and never hold a session. Passkeys (WebAuthn) are a
later stage; nothing here assumes they never come.

The maintainer settled the defaults on 2026-10-25: TOTP before
passkeys, `optional` as the instance default, the admin reset with
proof by mail, the factor after every first factor, good standing after
it, the step-up calls and window, and the limits below.

#### 2.8.1 Enrolment

Profile → Security → "Two-factor sign-in". Every human account may
enrol, with a password or without one: the factor is second to whatever
first factor the account uses. Enrolment needs the **proof** below and
the instance key
`MAITY_SECRET_KEY` (§16.2), which seals the secret at rest; without the
key the feature is unavailable (`GET /admin/settings/sign-in` names it
in `missing`, §2.6.6) and the calls below answer `409
secret_key_missing`.

| Endpoint | Caller | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /auth/second-factor` | human | `{enrolled, enrolled_at, recovery_codes_left, last_used_at, required}`; `required` is `true` when the instance policy makes this human enrol (§2.8.5), and after a reset until the human has enrolled again (§2.8.3) |
| `POST /auth/reauthenticate` `{password}` | human with a password | the password given again on the current session: 200 `{valid_until}`; wrong is `invalid` with `details.fields.password: "mismatch"`, counted against the login limit (§2.1) |
| `POST /auth/second-factor/totp` | human, with the proof below | starts an enrolment: 200 `{secret, otpauth_uri, expires_in: 600}`. `secret` is 20 random bytes in base32, `otpauth_uri` is `otpauth://totp/Maity:<handle>?secret=…&issuer=Maity&digits=6&period=30` (the issuer is the instance's public host when one is set). Shown this once; a new call replaces an unfinished one |
| `POST /auth/second-factor/totp/confirm` `{code}` | human, the same session | a current code from the app turns the enrolment on: 200 `{recovery_codes: [10 × "xxxxx-xxxxx"]}`, shown this once, and the session's `second_factor_at` is set (§2.8.4), so the code just used does not have to be followed by another. A wrong code is `code_invalid` (§2.8.6) and the enrolment stays unfinished until it expires |
| `POST /auth/second-factor/recovery-codes` | human, with the proof below, and step-up | ten new recovery codes, the old ones void at once; 200 `{recovery_codes}` |
| `DELETE /auth/second-factor` | human, with the proof below, and step-up | turns the second factor off for this human; `forbidden` with `details.reason: second_factor_required` while the policy requires it of this human (§2.8.5) |

- **The proof.** For an account **with a password**: the password,
  given in the last 10 minutes on the calling session — its sign-in by
  password, or `POST /auth/reauthenticate` — otherwise `forbidden` with
  `details.reason: reauthentication_required`. For an account
  **without one** (none can exist until the accounts design adds them:
  `POST /auth/register` and `maity-hub owner create` both set a
  password, §2.7.1): a session in good standing (§2.6.5) that is at
  least 24 hours old, the guard §2.6.3 sets for changing the verified
  address (not in good standing: `forbidden`, `details.reason:
  not_in_good_standing`; younger: `details.reason: session_too_new`).
  Never a fresh session from the mailbox: temporary access to the
  mailbox (§2.3) must not install a factor of its holder's choosing,
  which would give standing at the next sign-in (§2.8.2) and end the
  human's trusted sessions; and for a password account it would lock
  out the human who holds the password. How a passwordless account's
  first session comes to be in good standing — and with it how such an
  account enrols for the first time, under `required_admins` or after a
  reset — is the accounts design's item (pending), as is setting a
  first password on it; until that is settled, such a human without a
  session in good standing waits at the enrolment session (§2.8.5).
- **Enrolling again.** For a human who is already enrolled, `POST
  /auth/second-factor/totp` needs the proof and step-up (§2.8.4). The
  old secret and recovery codes stay valid until the confirm; the
  confirm replaces both, moves the generation (so outstanding reset
  links die), and writes `second_factor_changed` `{change: enrolled}`.
  Until then the human is never without a factor.
- **Existing sessions.** Enrolling leaves the human's other full
  sessions as they are — listed with `second_factor: false`, in good
  standing only if they already were — and the recovery-codes page
  offers "End my other sessions" (`POST /auth/sessions/end-others`).
- **The code.** RFC 6238 with SHA-1, 6 digits, a 30-second step; the
  current step and one step either side are accepted, and every step is
  accepted once per human (the hub stores the last step used), so a
  code read over a shoulder cannot be replayed. Spaces are ignored.
- **Recovery codes.** Ten, each ten characters of Crockford base32
  (`0-9` and `a-z` without `i`, `l`, `o`, `u`), 50 bits of randomness
  each, shown as `xxxxx-xxxxx`. On input case, spaces and the hyphen are
  ignored, and `i`, `l` read as `1`, `o` as `0`.
- **Storage.** The secret sealed with `MAITY_SECRET_KEY` (as the SMTP
  password, §16.2), never returned after the enrolment answer, never in
  a log or an event. Recovery codes stored as HMAC-SHA-256 under the
  same key, each usable once; a database copy alone yields neither.
- **The factor's generation.** Each human carries a counter that moves
  on every enrolment, turning off, reset, new set of recovery codes and
  use of a recovery code. A reset link names the generation it was
  issued for (§2.8.3).
- **The key lost.** While enrolments exist and `MAITY_SECRET_KEY` is
  missing or no longer opens them, the hub does **not** treat the
  instance as `off`: it fails closed. An enrolled human's sign-in stops
  at the second-factor session, whose verify answers `409
  secret_key_missing`, and `GET /admin/settings/sign-in` names
  `secret_key` in `missing` (§2.6.6). The operator restores the key, or
  resets humans one by one with `maity-hub second-factor reset`
  (§2.8.3), which needs no key. `required_admins` without the key would
  hold every admin at an enrolment session that can do nothing: the hub
  refuses to start with `MAITY_SIGN_IN_SECOND_FACTOR=required_admins` in
  the environment and no usable `MAITY_SECRET_KEY` (as §16.2 does for an
  invalid setting), and a `PATCH` to `required_admins` without it is
  `invalid` with `details.fields.second_factor: "secret_key_missing"`.
- **The QR** is drawn in the dashboard's own code from `otpauth_uri`,
  no third-party script or image service (§1.1, as the device code's
  QR in §2.6.7); the secret is also shown as text for manual entry.
- **Told.** Every change writes the account record
  `second_factor_changed` `{change, by}` (§18.1, a `security`
  notification) and sends the security mail of §18.5. `change` is
  `enrolled`, `disabled`, `recovery_codes`, `recovery_code_used`,
  `reset` or `instance_off`; `by` is the human's own handle for the
  first four, the admin's handle for a reset through the API,
  `operator` for `maity-hub second-factor reset`, and for
  `instance_off` the admin who switched it or `environment`. Turning
  the factor off also ends every other session of the human
  (`ended_by: second_factor_disabled`, §2.6.5).

#### 2.8.2 The sign-in step

For an enrolled human, every first factor — `POST /auth/login`, a
device code (§2.6.2), a sign-in link or code by mail (§2.6.3) — ends
in a **second-factor session** instead of a full one, the device code
included:

- The first factor answers as it does today, with `member` replaced by
  `{"second_factor": "required", "expires_in": 300}` (the login and the
  code redemptions answer 200; the link page's `POST` answers its `303`
  to the dashboard route `/sign-in/second-factor`, with `next` kept on
  the session). The cookies are set, the session exists, and its state
  is `second_factor`.
- A second-factor session reaches only `GET /auth/session` (which
  answers `{second_factor: "required", session_id, csrf_token,
  expires_at}` and no member — the verify carries the CSRF token as
  every cookie call),
  `POST /auth/second-factor/verify` and `POST /auth/logout`. Every other
  call is `forbidden` with `details.reason: second_factor_required`,
  before any side effect. It lives 5 minutes and is not listed in the
  session list.
- `POST /auth/second-factor/verify` `{code}` or `{recovery_code}`:
  right, and the hub ends the second-factor session and issues a
  **fresh** session id and CSRF token (§2.6.5's fixation rule applies at
  this moment, not at the first factor); 200 `{member, next}` as the
  login. Only now is the sign-in complete: `session_created` is written
  (§2.6.5) with `second_factor: totp | recovery_code`, the device
  cookie is set, `last_login_at` moves. A recovery code used here also
  writes `second_factor_changed` with `change: recovery_code_used` and
  `recovery_codes_left`.
- Wrong: `code_invalid`. The fifth wrong code ends the second-factor
  session (the first factor must be done again) and writes the account
  record `second_factor_failed` `{method, ip, browser, os}`, a
  `security` notification with a security mail: someone held the
  password, the mailbox or a device code, but not the app. At step-up
  (§2.8.4) the tenth wrong code in the window of §2.8.6, from whichever
  session, writes it too, with `method: step_up`.
- **What the second-factor session carries.** The first factor's
  `method`, its `approved_by` (the device-code session that approved
  it, with that session's own lineage for "End this session", §2.6.5),
  the stored `next` (§2.6.5), and the account's status: the full
  session the verify makes is the one the first factor would have made
  — a restricted pending session for an account that waits for approval
  (§2.7.5), with `method` and `approved_by` unchanged. The second
  factor adds to the existing rules, never replaces one.
- **One winner.** The verify is one transaction: the TOTP step is
  consumed only if it is newer than the last step used (a conditional
  update), a recovery code only if still unused, and the second-factor
  session is promoted only while it is still in that state. Of two
  concurrent verifies with the same code or the same session, one
  makes the full session; the other answers `code_invalid` and creates
  nothing.

**Good standing.** A session whose sign-in included the second factor
is in good standing (§2.6.5), whatever the first factor was: the factor
is what neither a mailbox nor an unlocked dashboard provides, which is
the reason good standing exists. The session list
carries `second_factor: true | false` per session.

#### 2.8.3 Recovery

A lost app is recovered with a recovery code at the sign-in step, then
a new enrolment from Profile → Security. Without a recovery code:

- **The instance admin resets it, with proof by mail.**
  `POST /admin/users/{id}/second-factor/reset` `{reason}` (scope
  `instance:admin`, human, step-up when the admin is enrolled) mails the
  human's verified address a link (§18.6, purpose
  `second_factor_reset`, 24 hours, single use, naming the factor's
  generation it was issued for, §2.8.1). The reset takes effect only
  when the human opens it and presses the button on its page, so an
  admin alone never strips a human's second factor. A link whose
  generation is no longer the human's is dead (§18.6): once the human
  recovered with a recovery code, enrolled anew, turned the factor off,
  or another reset took effect, every outstanding reset link is void, so
  an old link never removes a factor set up after it. Taking effect is
  one transaction — the link consumed, the generation checked and
  moved, the enrolment and the recovery codes deleted, every session of
  the human ended (`ended_by: second_factor_reset`, §2.6.5) — and of
  two links racing only the first succeeds. On
  effect: `second_factor_changed` `{change: reset, by: <admin
  handle>}` is written and the security mail of §18.5 sent, and the
  next sign-in of the human goes into enrolment (§2.8.5) whatever the
  policy says, unless it is `off`. An instance without mail cannot
  reset this way (`409 mail_not_configured`, §1.3), nor a human without
  a verified address (`409 address_unverified`). The mail proves the
  mailbox, not the person: the dashboard tells the admin to confirm the
  request with the person by another channel first, since whoever holds
  the mailbox is exactly who would ask for a reset.
- **The admin's own** is never reset through this endpoint
  (`forbidden`, `details.reason: own_account`): the admin uses a
  recovery code, or the operator's command below.
- **The operator** — the person with access to the server — has
  `maity-hub second-factor reset --handle <handle>`, which resets at
  once, moves the generation and writes the same record and mail (`by:
  operator`). It is the last way in, as `maity-hub owner create` is the
  first.
- A reset request is not an event; the accounts design's instance audit
  log records it (pending). Until then the human's account record is
  its trace.

#### 2.8.4 Step-up before sensitive calls

For an enrolled human the hub remembers on the session when the factor
was last given (`second_factor_at`): at the sign-in step, or with `POST
/auth/second-factor/verify` from a full session, which answers 200
`{valid_until}`; a recovery code is accepted there too and writes
`second_factor_changed` `{change: recovery_code_used}` as at the
sign-in step. A sensitive call needs it within the last **10
minutes**; otherwise it is `forbidden` with
`details.reason: step_up_required` and changes nothing, and the
dashboard asks for a code and repeats the call. A human who is not
enrolled is not asked, and nobody is while the instance setting is
`off` (§2.8.5).

The sensitive calls:

- changing or removing the verified address (§2.6.3, §18.4) and
  approving a held change;
- `POST /auth/password`;
- every change of the second factor itself (§2.8.1) and an admin reset
  (§2.8.3);
- calls that mint a credential or the means to one: creating a join
  (`POST /projects/{owner}/{slug}/joins`, §3.1) and a runner enrollment
  (`POST /runners/enrollments`, §15.2),
  and approving a device code (§2.6.2);
- transferring a project to another namespace owner (`POST
  /projects/{owner}/{slug}/transfer`, §6.25), including into an
  organisation and to oneself, and the `go` that consents to a transfer
  (`reply_id: go` on a `project_transfer` request, on the project's
  route and on the personal one of an organisation's owner, §6.26); a
  `no` needs none, since it moves nothing;
- deleting an organisation (`DELETE /orgs/{org}`, §6.26);
- giving the hub access to a forge account: `POST /me/forge/github/link`
  and `PUT /me/forge/github/token`, and confirming a project's repository
  for it (`POST /projects/{owner}/{slug}/repository/confirm`, §11.4);
- your own data: the export (`GET /me/export`) and a deletion request
  (`POST /me/deletion`, §2.9);
- the instance admin's changes of instance settings (`PATCH
  /admin/settings/*`, §2.6.6, §16).

A step-up never makes a session in good standing that was not (§2.6.5):
it proves the factor now, the standing rules keep their own record.

#### 2.8.5 The instance setting

A field of `GET, PATCH /admin/settings/sign-in` (§2.6.6), with the
environment winning as there:

| Environment | Field | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MAITY_SIGN_IN_SECOND_FACTOR` | `second_factor` | `optional` | `off`, `optional` or `required_admins` |

- **`off`.** The second factor is out of the way entirely: no sign-in
  step, no step-up (§2.8.4), no enrolment session, and the factor's own
  calls answer `forbidden` with `details.reason: method_disabled` —
  `POST /auth/second-factor/verify` included, which nothing then needs.
  Second-factor and enrolment sessions open at the switch end at their
  next call (`ended_by: second_factor_disabled`; the first factor is done again, and now gives a full
  session). Existing enrolments stay stored and apply again when the
  setting returns; each enrolled human gets a `second_factor_changed`
  `{change: instance_off}` record and security mail, so the switch
  cannot pass unnoticed. Sessions made while it was `off` stay when it
  returns, listed with `second_factor: false` and without the good
  standing the factor gives (§2.8.2); their next sensitive call asks for
  the factor (§2.8.4). A missing instance key is not `off` (§2.8.1).
- **`optional`.** Each human decides.
- **`required_admins`.** Instance admins and every human who owns a
  project must enrol. A sign-in of such a human who has not enrolled
  ends in an **enrolment session**: like a second-factor session
