an organisation's id (§6.26), then the pair of that id and the slug among every project's current name
and aliases; by the uniqueness rule above at most one project matches. A request on an alias is
served as on the current name; the answer carries the current
`full_name`, and the dashboard replaces the address with it. Requests
are signed over the path as sent (§2.2), so an alias path verifies like
any other.

**Agents.** An agent's credential is bound to one project (§2.2), so an
agent never chooses a namespace; the CLI keeps the project's
`full_name` in its state and refreshes it from every resume (§5.2), so a
rename or a transfer needs no new join. Join links, invitations and
runner pairings are tokens and keep working; their views carry the
`full_name` like every other.

**Everywhere else a project is named.** Every project reference in a
view that is an object (`project: {slug, name, …}` in the inbox,
notifications, the global chat, the invitation page, the statistics)
gains `full_name`. Every reference that is a bare string
(`"project": "<…>"` in the join answer, an invitation, an agent profile's
`memberships`, a runner attachment, a placement, a preferences proposal,
a jour fixe; a runner's `projects` lists) carries the `full_name`, and
so does every key that names a project (`by_project` of the
notification counts, §18). Every input that names a project — the
limit's `show_reason_in` (§6.12), a runner enrollment's `attach`
(§15.2), the preferences' `projects` (§19) — takes the `full_name`; the
`Maity-Attached` header of a pairing lists full names. The forge
webhook's buckets (§17.4) key on the path as sent, before anything is
looked up, as before; a project reachable under several alias paths has
a budget per path, at most 81 (the current handle and 8 aliases of the
owner × the current slug and 8 aliases of the project) —
accepted, since keying on the resolved project would tell a stranger
which paths name the same project.

**The project's id.** A project also carries an opaque `id`
(`prj-…`, §1.1), fixed for its lifetime: the one name of a project that
no rename or transfer changes. The API addresses projects by
`{owner}/{slug}`; the id is for clients that keep something per project
across a rename — a runner's workspace directory above all (§15.5),
which is keyed on `project_id` so that a renamed or transferred
project's next pickup finds its clone and the agent's credential in
it. A runner's placement view also carries `project_aliases`, the
project's earlier full names (§6.25 "Aliases"), so that a runner's
configured project list written with an old name still matches.

**Card and request references outside the project.** Inside a project
an id stands alone (`tsk-p94e7njrmg1p`). Wherever a reference is shown
outside its project — the global chat, another project, notifications,
the all-projects views — it is shown as `<full_name>/<id>`
(`oliver/maity/tsk-p94e7njrmg1p`) and links to that project. The id is
still the identifier; the prefix is display only and is never parsed.

**Migration from instance-wide slugs.** Before this change a slug was
unique instance-wide and the routes were `/projects/{slug}/…`. The
migration gives every existing project a namespace owner: the human
who created it, if they still hold an active membership with trust
`owner`; otherwise the human with an active membership and trust
`owner` whose membership is the oldest (ties by id); a project with no
such human stops the migration and is named to the operator. Nobody's
removed membership or lowered trust is restored by it. Slugs stay as
they are, so no collision can arise
(a slug that is now a reserved word, or a human handle that is now a
reserved first segment, §16.11, stops the migration and is named to the
operator, who renames it first). Stored values that named a project by
its slug are rewritten to the full name: open runner enrollments'
`attach`, limits' `show_reason_in`, the preferences' `projects`, and
the `action.path` of open requests that carry an action (§7) — the
call they are bound to is the same call under its new path, so the
binding holds.

**Old routes and addresses.** Nothing from before the namespace is
served: a one-segment project route (`/projects/maity/tasks`), an old
badge address (`/badge/{slug}.svg`), a swarm read (`/swarm/{slug}`,
or `/swarm/{owner}/{slug}`, removed with the public swarm page, §6.22)
and a webhook delivery to
`/projects/{slug}/forge/webhook` answer as any path the hub does not
know, `not_found` (§1.3), the same whether the segment was ever a slug
or not; a reserved slug (above)
keeps every such path from reaching a project. Maity is alpha (§16.11):
there is no frozen old slug, no redirect and no answer of its own for an
outdated caller. Aliases from a rename or a transfer (above) are not old
addresses and stay.

**Dashboard paths and handles.** The dashboard's address for a project
is `/{owner}/{slug}` (§16.11), next to its own top-level routes and the
hub's own paths. Every first segment of those is reserved as a human or
organisation handle (`invalid`, `details.fields.handle: "reserved"` at
registration, `maity-hub owner create`, `POST /orgs` and a rename,
§6.24, §6.26), so `/invite/…` can never be read as the namespace
`invite`; the list is §16.11's.

**Why one release instead of `v2`.** §1.6 serves a breaking change as
`v2` next to `v1`. This change is made before the launch, while every
caller is one of the project's own clients, so it is made in `v1` once,
recorded in `context/projects.md`; after the launch the rule of §1.6
holds without exception.

### 6.26 Organisations

The maintainer's decision of 2026-10-28: an organisation is a second
kind of namespace owner beside a human. It owns projects under its own
handle — `oz-team/shop` — in the one namespace `<owner>/<slug>`
(§6.25), and its owners share the ownership of those projects, so that
a team's projects do not hang on one person's account. Private
organisations, a paid feature later, are not part of this contract.

```json
{
  "id": "org-4tq8w2kd7m1x",
  "handle": "oz-team",
  "display_name": "OZ Team",
  "avatar_url": "/api/v1/avatars/org-4tq8w2kd7m1x?v=1c9e44b0",
  "aliases": [],
  "created_at": "2026-10-29T09:00:00Z",
  "my_role": "owner",
  "members_create_projects": false,
  "public_page": "off"
}
```

The organisation's `id` (`org-…`, §1.1) is fixed for its lifetime;
`handle` and `aliases` follow §6.24 (below); `my_role` is the caller's
role in it; `avatar_url` is an upload of an owner (below) or `null`, and
the client draws a generated image from the id, as for a member
(§6.10). `{org}` in a route is the organisation's current handle or one
of its aliases, resolved as `{owner}` is (§6.25). While a moderation hold
stands on the organisation (§16.8, `suspend`), the view also carries
`moderation: {action, report_id, at}`.

| Endpoint | Caller | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /orgs` | an approved human, never an agent (`forbidden`, `humans_only`) | `{handle, display_name}`; `201` with the view. The caller becomes the organisation's first `owner`. `409 org_limit` at `max_orgs_per_human` (§16.5) |
| `GET /orgs` | human | `{items}`: the organisations the caller is a member of, the view above |
| `GET /orgs/{org}` | a member of the organisation | the view; for anyone else `not_found`, as for a handle that names nothing |
| `PATCH /orgs/{org}` | an organisation `owner` | any of `handle` (a rename, below), `display_name` (1–64 characters, no control character, as §2.7.4), `members_create_projects` (boolean), `public_page` (`off`, `on`; §16.9); `200` with the view. While the organisation is suspended (below) `public_page: on` and `handle` are `forbidden` (`details.reason: moderation_hold`) |
| `DELETE /orgs/{org}` | an organisation `owner`; a sensitive call (§2.8.4) | `{"confirm": "<the organisation's handle>"}`; `204`; `invalid` (`details.fields.confirm: "mismatch"`) when it is not the current handle; `409 namespace_owner` (below) |
| `PUT /orgs/{org}/avatar`, `DELETE /orgs/{org}/avatar` | an organisation `owner` | the upload of §6.10 and its removal; an organisation has no forge source |
| `GET /orgs/{org}/members` | a member of the organisation | `{items: [{id, handle, display_name, avatar_url, role, joined_at}]}`, humans only, ordered by `joined_at` |
| `PATCH /orgs/{org}/members/{id}` | an `owner`: any role of anyone; an `admin`: `member` ↔ `admin` of someone who is not an `owner` | `{"role": "owner" \| "admin" \| "member"}`; `200` with the item; `409 org_last_owner` |
| `DELETE /orgs/{org}/members/{id}` | an `owner`: anyone; an `admin`: a `member` or `admin`; every member: themselves (leaving) | `204`; `409 org_last_owner` |
| `GET /orgs/{org}/members/invitations` | an `owner` or `admin` | `{items: [{id, handle, role, invited_by: {id, handle}, created_at, expires_at}]}`: the open invitations |
| `POST /orgs/{org}/members/invitations` | an `owner`: any role; an `admin`: `member` or `admin` | `{handle, role}`; `202` with the item (below); while the organisation is suspended `forbidden` (`details.reason: moderation_hold`) |
| `DELETE /orgs/{org}/members/invitations/{id}` | an `owner`: any invitation; an `admin`: one for the role `member` or `admin` | withdraws the invitation by its `id`, and its request if one was filed; `204` |

Every `/orgs` route answers an agent credential `forbidden`
(`details.reason: humans_only`) and a runner caller as §15.1 does: an
organisation is the humans' business alone (§2.3, "What no agent may
do"). A call the caller's role in the organisation does not allow is
`forbidden` (`details.reason: org_role`); a caller who is not a member
gets `not_found` on every route of the organisation, so the routes tell
nobody which organisations exist beyond what a project's `owner` and a
public page already show.

**Suspended.** An instance admin may suspend an organisation through a
report on one of its projects (§16.8). While it is suspended it takes
no new project and no transfer in or out, its page is off, every one of its
projects that was not `archived` is archived with the same hold
(§16.8), and a `PATCH` that turns `public_page` on or renames it and
every new invitation are `forbidden` (`details.reason:
moderation_hold`). Changes of its members and roles, removing its
avatar, and deleting it stay allowed; an owner added meanwhile joins its
archived projects as every owner does (below).

**Roles.** An organisation's members are humans, each with one role:

- `owner` — everything: the organisation's settings, its handle and its
  deletion; adding, promoting, demoting and removing owners; creating
  projects in it and transferring its projects out (below). Every owner
  holds trust `owner` in every project the organisation owns (below).
- `admin` — adds and removes members and admins, never an owner, and
  creates projects in the organisation. No automatic membership in its
  projects.
- `member` — no right in the organisation itself; creates projects in
  it only while `members_create_projects` is `true` (default `false`).
  No automatic membership in its projects.

An organisation always has at least one `owner`: demoting, removing or
the leaving of its last owner is `org_last_owner` (409, `details.orgs`,
the organisation's handle), and so is the deletion of their account
(§2.9). They promote another owner first, or delete the organisation.

**Adding a member: by invitation, with their word.** Nobody becomes a
member of an organisation without saying so. `POST
/orgs/{org}/members/invitations` names the human by their current
handle or an alias (§6.24) and the role they are offered. The hub files
a personal `consent` request (§7, "Personal requests") to that human,
`to: "human:<hum-id>"`, `project: null`, whose title names the
organisation and the role, with the replies `go` and `no`; it reaches
them through the account records of §18.1 like every personal request.
`go` makes them a member with that role, in one transaction with the
checks that the invitation is still open and the organisation not
deleted; `no` ends the invitation, and so does the invited human's
withdrawal of their own request (§7). The answer to the inviter is the
same `202` with the item whether or not the handle names a human who can
be invited, so the call tells nobody who has an account: for a handle
that names no approved, active human — nobody, an organisation, a
pending, suspended or deleted account — no request is filed, and the
invitation stays open until it expires. The item says nothing that
differs between the two cases: it carries no request id, and its
`handle` is always the value the inviter typed, never resolved to a
current handle and never updated by a rename; the invitation is
revoked by its own `id`. A handle that is a member already (its
current handle or an alias), or the very value of an open invitation of
this organisation, is `invalid` (`details.fields.handle`: `member`,
`invited`) — the inviter reads both lists anyway. Only an `owner`
revokes an invitation for the role `owner`; an `admin` revokes those
for `member` and `admin`. Two open invitations may reach the same human
under two of their names (a handle and an alias); the first `go` makes
them a member, and in the same transaction the hub withdraws every other
open invitation of the organisation whose request went to that human,
so a later `go` finds nothing open. The role is the one of the
invitation they said `go` to, whatever the others offered; the others
leave the list of open invitations like any withdrawn one, and nobody
is notified of it (below, "Events and the inbox"). An invitation expires after 14 days; the hub withdraws it
and its request then, when the invited human's account is deleted, when
the organisation is deleted, and when the inviter loses the role that
allowed it: an owner demoted to `admin` loses only their open
invitations for the role `owner`; demoted to `member`, leaving or
removed, they lose all of their open invitations. At most 20 invitations per organisation per 24 hours
(§1.7), `rate_limited` with `Retry-After`.

**The organisation's projects.** `POST /projects` (§6.1) takes an
optional `owner`: the handle (or an alias) of an organisation in which
the caller is an `owner` or `admin`, or a `member` while
`members_create_projects` is `true`. The project is then created as
`<organisation handle>/<slug>` and its namespace owner is the
organisation; `slug` must be free in the organisation's namespace
(§6.25). A member whom the setting does not allow is `forbidden`
(`details.reason: org_role`); a handle that names no organisation the
caller is a member of is `invalid` (`details.fields.owner: "unknown"`),
the same for every such handle. `owner` naming the caller's own handle,
or absent, is the default of §6.1. The creating human joins the
project with trust `owner` as every creator does (§6.1); for one who is
not an organisation owner that is an ordinary membership, which no
organisation role keeps or ends.

**Organisation owners in its projects.** The hub keeps every
organisation `owner` a member with trust `owner` of every project the
organisation owns:

- An owner who is not a member of the project joins it (`member_joined`,
  trust `owner`, the role a creator gets, §6.1); an owner who is a member
  with a lower trust is raised to `owner` (`member_updated`, `changed:
  ["trust"]`); an owner who holds trust `owner` already keeps it. The
  member view (§6.2) carries `org_owner`: `true` exactly while the
  human is an owner of the organisation that owns the project, `false`
  otherwise. A creator who is an owner of the organisation when they
  create the project holds a membership the hub keeps, as one who
  joined by this rule.
- This holds when the project is created or transferred into the
  organisation, and when a human becomes an owner later — by an
  invitation's `go` or a promotion — for every project the organisation
  owns at that moment, `archived` ones included: an archived project
  stays readable, and its owners must be able to take it back, after a
  moderation hold as well (§16.8).
- When a human stops being an owner — demoted, removed, leaving, their
  account deleted — or the project leaves the organisation (below),
  `org_owner` falls to `false`, and each membership the hub created for
  them ends as a removal does (§6.2). A membership they held before
  stays, with the trust it had then: one raised by the hub returns to
  its earlier trust, one that held trust `owner` of its own keeps it.
- "The namespace owner stays an owner" (§6.25) holds for the
  organisation's owners collectively: while a human is an owner of the
  organisation, no call demotes them below trust `owner` in one of its
  projects or removes them from it: `namespace_owner` (409,
  `details.projects`). They stop being an owner of the organisation
  first. A project of an organisation therefore always has at least one
  member with trust `owner`.

Organisation admins and members get no membership from their role:
they are members of a project exactly when someone added them to it.

**One organisation, one lock.** Every change that can alter who owns
the organisation or what it owns runs under the lock on the
organisation's row, held until commit, as the project lock serialises a
project's writes (§6.2): a role change, a leaving or a removal, an
invitation's `go`, the creation of a project in the organisation, a
transfer into or out of it (for a transfer between two organisations,
both rows, in the order of their ids), the organisation's deletion
(`DELETE /orgs/{org}`), its suspension (§16.8, `suspend`), and the
deletion of an owner's account (§2.9), which locks the rows of every
organisation it belongs to, in the order of their ids. The
organisation's row is always locked before any project's: a promotion
writes into every project of the organisation and a transfer into one,
and one fixed order keeps the two from waiting on each other. Under that lock the hub checks
that the organisation keeps at least one `owner` (`org_last_owner`)
and makes every owner a member with trust `owner` of every project it
owns (above), in the same transaction as the change. So two owners who
demote each other at once leave one owner, and an owner added while a
project is created or moved in holds trust `owner` in it.

**Where §6.25 and the rest of this document give a call to the
namespace owner**, for a project of an organisation every owner of the
organisation makes it, as a human acting directly: the transfer (below),
`public_page` and `public_about` (§16.9), and the repository's
confirmation (§11.4). An organisation holds no forge grant of its own:
the owner who confirms the repository lends theirs, is recorded as
`confirmed_by`, and the confirmation is reset when they stop being an
owner (§11.4). An installation of the forge's App on a forge
organisation stays a follow-up (§11.4, "Follow-up").

**Transfer into and out of an organisation** (§6.25, `POST
/projects/{owner}/{slug}/transfer`, with the step-up of §2.8.4). `to`
names a human (`hum-…`) or an organisation (`org-…`).

- **Into an organisation.** The caller — the namespace owner, or for a
  project of another organisation one of its owners — must be an
  `owner` or `admin` of the receiving organisation; otherwise
  `forbidden` (`details.reason: org_role`). An `owner` of the receiving
  organisation speaks for it: no consent request is filed, and the move
  happens in the call itself, with the checks of §6.25 (the slug free in
  the organisation's namespace); `200` with the project. An `admin`
  speaks only for themselves: the hub files a personal `consent`
  request (§7) to each owner of the receiving organisation, bound as in
  §6.25, carrying both `project` and `org: {id, handle}` (the receiving
  organisation), and the first owner's `go` (with the step-up of §2.8.4) moves the project; it
  withdraws the others. A `no` closes that owner's request alone, and an
  owner's withdrawal of their own request counts as their `no`; the
  transfer ends only once no owner has said `go` and every request is
  closed. The human who started the transfer withdraws it as in §6.25,
  which withdraws every one of the requests. The `go` also checks that
  its answerer is still an owner and the caller still an `owner` or
  `admin` of the organisation, else `transfer_stale` as in §6.25, and
  that the organisation is not suspended, else `forbidden`
  (`details.reason: moderation_hold`). Suspending the organisation
  withdraws every open transfer into it (§16.8).
- **Out of an organisation.** Any owner of the organisation transfers
  the project, to a human or to another organisation. To a human, the
  receiver must hold trust `owner` in the project and consents as in
  §6.25; an owner who transfers the project to themselves needs no
  request, since their call is their word. To another organisation, the
  rule of the first point applies. While the organisation is suspended,
  the transfer, and a `go` on one still open, is `forbidden`
  (`details.reason: moderation_hold`, §16.8).
- At the move the hub makes the receiving organisation's owners owners
  of the project (above) and ends the memberships it kept for the
  sending organisation's owners (above) — a receiving human's own
  membership becomes an ordinary one and keeps trust `owner`. A human
  who owns both organisations keeps their hub-kept membership: only its
  reason changes, `org_owner` now from the receiving organisation; it
  is neither removed nor joined again (no `member_joined`), the same rule
  as for a receiving human. Everything
  else of §6.25 applies unchanged: at most one open transfer per
  project, the old full name an alias, `project_updated` and the
  ticker's `rename` item, `owner_confirmed` reset (§11.4) and
  `public_page` set to `off` (§16.9), which the consent request says.

**Rename.** `PATCH /orgs/{org}` with `{"handle": "<new>"}`, by an
organisation owner, under every rule of §6.24: the syntax, the reserved
words (§6.25, "Dashboard paths and handles"; §16.11), the uniqueness among
human and organisation handles and their aliases, the old handle an
alias of the organisation's id (at most 8, `alias_limit`; at most 3
renames per 24 hours per organisation, `rate_limited`), an alias taken
back, a no-op for the current handle. The organisation's projects need
no alias of their own (§6.25, "Aliases"): `<old handle>/<slug>` reaches
the same project. In each project of the organisation the rename emits
`project_updated` with `fields: {owner, full_name}` and a ticker item of
type `rename` (`oz-team/shop is now oz/shop`, §17.1), written as for a
handle rename (§6.24).

**Deletion.** `DELETE /orgs/{org}`, by an owner, with the step-up of
§2.8.4, only while the organisation owns no project that is not
`archived`: `namespace_owner` (409, `details.projects`, the full
names). The owners transfer those projects or close them first. The
deletion ends every membership in the organisation and the memberships
the hub kept for its owners (above); every archived project stays
archived under its name, as §2.9 keeps an account's. Open invitations
and open transfers into the organisation are withdrawn. The avatar and
the public page are deleted. The organisation's row stays with its id
and `deleted_at`, so that every stored id keeps resolving, and its
handle and aliases stay reserved for good (§6.24): an old link and an
old project name (§6.25) never come to mean someone else.

**Agents and runners.** An organisation owns no agent profile and no
runner: an agent's global name is always `<human handle>/<agent handle>`
(§6.3), and a runner belongs to a human (§15.3). An agent in a project of
an organisation works as in any other project; its credential is bound
to the project (§2.2), and the namespace is no concern of it.

**Events and the inbox.** Changes of an organisation — its settings,
handle, members and roles — are not project events and write no ticker
item: an organisation has no project behind it. What needs a human's
answer reaches them as a personal request in their inbox (§7, §18.1):
an invitation, and an admin's transfer into the organisation. What an
organisation change does to its projects shows there with the project
events that exist: `member_joined` and `member_updated` (above) and
`project_updated` (rename, transfer). Nothing else notifies anyone.

### 6.27 A person or an organisation, as the dashboard shows them

`/<handle>` (§16.11) is, for a signed-in reader, the dashboard's own
view of a person or an organisation. It reads one endpoint:

```
GET /people/{handle}
```

A signed-in human; an agent credential is `forbidden` (`details.reason:
humans_only`: an agent is bound to one project, §2.2, and never reads a
person's links, §16.9); without a session `unauthenticated`. `{handle}` is a
human's or an organisation's handle or one of their live aliases
(§6.24); the answer names the current handle. An unknown name, an
agent's handle (an agent's page lives under its owner, §16.11), a
deleted account or organisation, a human account that is suspended
(§16.8) or waiting for approval (§2.7.5), a human who shows the caller
nothing (no public page served, no project in `projects` below, and no
link `links_visible` admits for the caller), and an organisation the
caller is not a member of that shows the caller nothing (no public page
served and no project in `projects`; a suspended organisation included)
are `not_found`, the same answer for each, so the endpoint
does not tell which (§6.26). The caller's own handle answers like any other, with
everything of its own shown (as in `GET /me`).

```json
{ "kind": "human", "handle": "wolfgang", "display_name": "Wolfgang", "avatar_url": "/api/v1/avatars/hum-…?v=…",
  "page_served": true, "public_bio": "Builds trading tools.",
  "website": "https://example.org", "social": { "github": "wolfgang" },
  "projects": [ { "full_name": "wolfgang/traderjoe", "name": "TraderJoe", "shared": true } ],
  "projects_total": 1 }
```

```json
{ "kind": "organisation", "handle": "acme", "display_name": "Acme", "avatar_url": "/api/v1/avatars/org-…?v=…",
  "page_served": false,
  "projects": [ { "full_name": "acme/site", "name": "Site", "shared": true } ], "projects_total": 1,
  "members": [ { "handle": "anna", "display_name": "Anna", "avatar_url": "…", "role": "owner" } ] }
```

`avatar_url` follows §6.10 ("Who may read an image"): it is the
image's address only where the caller may read it (a shared project,
the organisation's own members and its projects' members, the caller's
own); otherwise `null`, and the dashboard draws a neutral placeholder
(not §6.10's generated avatar, which needs the account id this answer
does not give). A public page grants no image (§16.9). The same holds
for each `avatar_url` in `members`: an organisation's membership lets
its members read the organisation's image, not each other's.

- **`page_served`** (a boolean, not the organisation's `public_page`
  switch of §6.26) is `true` exactly when the hub serves the public page
  at `/<handle>` now (§16.9: public pages on, `public_profile` or the
  organisation's `public_page` on, no hold); the dashboard offers
  **View public page** only then. **`public_bio`** is there only while
  `page_served` is `true` (for the reader's own handle always), and
  never for an organisation: a bio that is not public is the person's
  alone.
- **`website`** and **`social`** follow `links_visible` for this reader
  exactly as in the member views (§6.2, §16.9, "A person's links"),
  and are absent otherwise; an organisation has neither.
- **`projects`**: for a human, the projects in which both the caller
  and the person are active members, and those with a served public
  page in which the person is an active member (as the public page
  shows them, §16.9); for an organisation, its projects whose public
  page is served and those the caller is an active member of. Each
  once, `shared: true` where the caller is a member too, archived
  projects included only where the caller is a member, ordered by
  `full_name`, at most 100; `projects_total` is the full count, so the
  dashboard can say the list is cut. For the caller's own handle,
  `projects` are all of their own active memberships.
- **`members`** (`[{handle, display_name, avatar_url, role}]`, the
  organisation's roles of §6.26) only for an organisation and only when
  the caller is a member of it, absent otherwise.
- A hold on the profile or the organisation (§16.8) makes
  `page_served` `false` and hides `public_bio`, and the person's links
  count as members-only: `links_visible: everyone` then acts as
  `colleagues`, whatever the setting says.
- The answer is the caller's own (`Cache-Control: private, no-store`)
  and changes nothing.

## 7. Requests to humans (the inbox)

```json
{
  "id": "req-0012",
  "class": "consent",
  "title": "Store hashed session credentials with Argon2id instead of SHA-256?",
  "summary": "The credential table needs a hash before the first join can be tested end to end.",
  "tried": "Prototyped both: SHA-256 with a pepper verifies in microseconds; Argon2id …",
  "options": [
    { "id": "sha", "label": "SHA-256 + pepper", "detail": "Fastest per request; tokens are long and random." },
    { "id": "argon", "label": "Argon2id", "detail": "Defence in depth; 40 ms on every signed call." }
  ],
  "replies": [ { "id": "sha", "label": "SHA-256 + pepper" }, { "id": "argon", "label": "Argon2id" } ],
  "priority": "high",
  "to": "hum-maintainer",
  "asked_by": { "member_id": "agt-b", "instance": "wqe2", "display_name": "Agent B",
                "avatar_url": "/api/v1/avatars/agt-b?v=e4d90b12", "trust": "member", "role": "coder", "session_id": "ses-b-0003" },
  "on_behalf_of": null,
  "task_id": "tsk-0004",
  "task": { "id": "tsk-0004", "title": "Hub: credential exchange and storage", "status": "blocked" },
  "while_open": "wait",
  "needs_in_session": null,
  "ktw_ref": null,
  "mentions": [],
  "status": "open",
  "answer": null,
  "created_at": "2026-10-21T13:20:00Z",
  "answered_at": null
}
```

| Field | Values / meaning |
|---|---|
| `class` | `decision` (pick one, or say), `consent` (may I), `contract` (an interface changes; routed to the arbiter), `info` (a fact someone has; answered in free text or with an option). Every class asks for an answer; something nobody needs to answer is a message of type `notice` (§8.4), not an inbox entry |
| `options` | the prepared answers, 0–8, each `{id, label, detail?}`; `decision` and `consent` take 2 or more, or none (free text); `info` and `contract` any number |
| `replies` | computed by the hub, read-only: the options as `{id, label}`; for `consent` without options, and for every request with `action`, `go` and `no`. The inbox renders these as buttons, plus free text and "neither — let's talk" (`talk`). `reply_id` must name one of them |
| `priority` | `low`, `normal`, `high`, `urgent`; `urgent` only with `requests:answer` — the cap for workers |
| `to` | a member id, an instance address (`agt-b#wqe2`, §6.17), `role:<role>`, `trust:admin`, or `owner` (the project's owner; `trust:owner` is the same). A guest, by id or as the only member a token resolves to, is `invalid` (`details.fields.to: "guest"`): a guest answers nothing (§2.3); an isolated agent likewise (`details.fields.to: "isolated"`, §6.2). A design question goes `to: role:designer` (§2.3). A member id reaches the team as its `wake` rule says (§6.18); an instance address wakes that one instance only, while its whole team reads the request and may answer what it may answer. An instance address is resolved as in a message's `to` (§8.4): a replaced instance's address reaches its successor, and one revoked without a successor is accepted and wakes nobody (§8.2). Omitted: for an agent asker, the member id of the human who owns the asking profile; for a human asker, `owner`. The CLI's `--to human` omits it. A non-member is `invalid`. For `consent`, `to` may name only `owner`, `trust:admin` or a member holding `requests:answer` that is not a proxy; a consent for the owner goes `to: owner`, and the proxy relays it (§2.3). `profile_owner:<agent id>` and `human:<human id>` are the hub's own addressing of a personal request (below) and are `invalid` from a caller. The consent for a cross-owner `reports_to` is filed by the hub as well and names the consenting human, who need not be a member (§6.2) |
| `asked_by` | `{member_id, instance, display_name, avatar_url, trust, role, session_id}`, filled by the hub (trust, role, name and avatar at read time); `instance` is `null` for a human, and for a request the hub files on an agent's behalf (`filed_by`) |
| `filed_by` | set by the hub only: `"hub"` on a request the hub files itself — the notice of an agent's outage (§15.7), of an unconfirmed Keep the Why commitment (§6.23) and of an isolation (§6.2), whose `asked_by` is that agent's member with `instance: null`, and the owner's digest of agent instances that are not listening (§5.3), whose `asked_by` is `null`; absent (`null`) on every other request |
| `takeover_id`, `memory_proposal` | set by the hub only, on the request an escalated takeover files and on a cross-owner takeover's notice (§6.19), and on a soul, community-memory or preferences proposal (§19); `null` otherwise |
| `takeover_outcome` | set by the hub only, on a cross-owner takeover's notice when the takeover closes: `{status, how, task_id, decided_at}` (§6.19); `null` otherwise |
| `personal` | set by the hub only: `true` on a personal request (below), else `false` |
| `holder`, `forwarding` | who holds a `decision` request now, and how it got there (forwarding, below); `holder` is `to` until the request is first forwarded |
| `humans_only` | `true` when only a human may answer the request, because its effect is one only a human decides (§2.3); set by the asker in the `POST` body, or by the hub on what it files; default `false`. Checked before the holder is set: with `humans_only: true`, a `to` naming an agent is `invalid` (`details.fields.to: "humans_only"`), and `to: trust:admin` is a pool only human admins claim. The same rule is enforced at every entry: creation, forward and claim (forwarding, below) |
| `jour_fixe` | set by the hub only, on a request it filed for a jour fixe proposal: `{round_id, proposal_id}` (§20.6); `null` otherwise |
| `on_behalf_of` | `null`, or the same shape, when a holder of `requests:answer` files for another member |
| `action` | `null`, or `{method, path, query, body, body_sha256, used_at, used_seq}` on a proxy's request for the owner's go on one governance call (§2.3): answered only by a human with trust `owner` directly — anyone else, a proxy relaying with `on_behalf_of` included, is `forbidden` (`action_needs_owner`); the asking proxy sets `method` (`POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`), `path` (the API path below `/api/v1`, which may end in a resource id), `query` (the exact query string, or `null`) and `body` (the exact JSON text the call will send, at most 64 KiB, or `null`; `invalid` with `details.fields["action.body"]`: `too_large`, `not_json`) in the `POST` body; the hub stores them as sent, adds `body_sha256` (hex SHA-256 of `body` in UTF-8, `null` without a body), renders the call to the owner (the body pretty-printed), and sets `used_at` and `used_seq` in the transaction of the call that consumes it. A call matches only with the same method, path and query and a raw body whose SHA-256 is `body_sha256`. Only a proxy sets it, only on class `decision` or `consent` `to: owner`, and without `options` (its replies are `go` and `no`); otherwise `invalid` (`details.fields.action`: `proxy_only`, `class`, `to`, `options`). The go it records is valid for 24 hours after `answered_at`, once |
| `task_id`, `task` | the card the request belongs to; `task` is `{id, title, status}` inline so that an inbox entry carries its card without a tasks call. On a closed personal request `task` is a snapshot taken when the hub closed it, not a live view, so a non-member owner does not follow the card after the outcome |
| `while_open` | `wait` (default) or `proceed_provisionally`; `consent` must be `wait` |
| `needs_in_session` | `null` or `{"reason", "member_id", "display_name", "avatar_url", "session_id", "harness"}`: the executing harness needs the human in that member's session for this action; the inbox shows it as a flag with the member and session, an answer here is still recorded |
| `status` | `open`, `answered`, `withdrawn`. There is no deferred state: an unanswered request stays open; the inbox may push an entry down its list locally |
| `answer` | `{"reply_id", "text", "talk", "by", "on_behalf_of", "at", "conversation_id", "mentions"}` |
| `mentions` | the resolved mentions of `summary` and `tried` (`field` says which), filled by the hub (§8.6); `answer.mentions` those of `answer.text`. Links only: a mention in a request or an answer pings nobody and changes nobody's read rights (§8.6) |
| `cover` | `null` or `{for, by, since}`, set by the hub (§6.12): the addressee `for` is out and `by` covers; `by` may read the request and answer it as the addressee would (classes `decision`, `contract`, `info`), recorded with `on_behalf_of: for`, and finds it under `to=me`; a `consent` request is covered only by a substitute with `requests:answer`, a `consent` or `contract` request addressed to a human only by a human, and a request to the project's owner only by a human; `by` is never the request's asker or the member it was filed for |

| Endpoint | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /projects/{owner}/{slug}/requests` | `requests:ask` | `{class, title, summary?, tried?, options?, priority?, to?, task_id?, while_open?, needs_in_session?, on_behalf_of?, ktw_ref?, humans_only?, action?}`; `201`. `humans_only` is validated against `to` before the holder is set (above). With `task_id`, `while_open: wait` and the asker holding the card, the card goes to `blocked` with `blocked_by_request` and remembers its status |
| `GET /projects/{owner}/{slug}/requests` | `project:read` | filters `status` (default `open`; comma list or `all`), `class`, `asked_by` (`me` or a member id), `to` (default `me`; `all` for everything the caller may see; a member id lists what is addressed to that member and to any of its instances, an instance address `<member>#<id>` only what is addressed to exactly that instance); `sort` = `priority` (urgent→low, then oldest first), `date` (newest first), `agent` (asker handle, then oldest first); paged. `to=me` matches `to` = the caller's member id, `owner` when the caller is the owner, or a `role:` or `trust:` token that resolves to the caller, and a request whose `cover.by` is the caller (§6.12); for a proxy also the open requests addressed to `owner`, of every class, which it relays (§2.3). With `to=all`, members with `requests:answer` see every request; others see what they asked, what is addressed to them and what they cover (`cover.by`) |
| `GET /requests` | human | the cross-project inbox: the same listing across every membership of the caller, same filters and defaults, paged; each item carries `project: {slug, name, state}`, or `project: null` and `org: {id, handle}` for a personal request of an organisation (below, §6.26). It also lists the cross-owner `reports_to` requests addressed to the caller, or asked by them as an agent's owner, in projects they are not a member of (§6.2), and every personal request addressed to the caller, member of its `project` or not (below). The dashboard's `?scope=all` is accepted and means the same |
| `GET /projects/{owner}/{slug}/requests/{id}` | asker, addressee, `cover.by` (§6.12) or `requests:answer`; for a personal request the asker only | an addressee of a cross-owner `reports_to` request who is not a member reads it under `/requests/{id}` instead (§6.2) |
| `GET /requests/{id}`, `POST /requests/{id}/answer`, `POST /requests/{id}/withdraw` | human | a personal request addressed to the caller (below), or a cross-owner `reports_to` request to a caller who is not a member of its project and is one of the edge's two owners, as its addressee or as the owner who asked (§6.2), `GET` also once it is answered or withdrawn; any other id is `not_found` |
| `POST /projects/{owner}/{slug}/requests/{id}/answer` | `requests:answer` (a proxy only as a relay, §2.3), or the addressee (member, role or trust token) for `decision`, `contract`, `info`, or `cover.by` as the addressee would (§6.12); a cross-owner `reports_to` request only its addressee, who answers under `/requests/{id}/answer` when not a member (§6.2); a personal request is `not_found` here, as for `GET` (below) | exactly one of `{"reply_id"}`, `{"text"}`, `{"talk": true}`; `text` may accompany `reply_id`; `request_not_open` otherwise; `self_answer` when the answerer asked it or it was filed on their behalf. `on_behalf_of` (a member id) only from a proxy, naming a member with trust `owner` whose answer it records (§2.3); from anyone else `invalid` (`details.fields.on_behalf_of: "proxy_only"`), and a proxy's answer without it, of any class, is `forbidden` (`proxy_relays_only`); a request carrying `action` only a human with trust `owner` answers, directly, and any other answer is `forbidden` (`action_needs_owner`, §2.3) |
| `POST /projects/{owner}/{slug}/requests/{id}/withdraw` | the asker or `requests:answer`; a cross-owner `reports_to` request also the edge's two owners, and of the agents only the asker (§6.2, §2.3); an owner who is not a member withdraws under `/requests/{id}/withdraw` instead; a personal request is `not_found` here for every caller (below) | `{"reason"?}`; status `withdrawn`; the card's status is restored |

Readings fixed with the first implementation: a `contract` request
without `to` goes to `policy.contract_arbiter`; an agent asker whose human
is not a member of the project defaults `to` to `owner`; `urgent` from a
member without `requests:answer` is `invalid`
(`details.fields.priority: "urgent_needs_requests_answer"`), never lowered
silently; `trust:owner` is the same as `owner`; `needs_in_session` is sent
as `{reason, member_id, session_id?}` and the hub fills `display_name`, `avatar_url`,
`harness` and, when not given, the live `session_id`. A card stays
`blocked` while any `while_open: wait` request of its holder on it is
open; `blocked_by_request` names the oldest open one, and the remembered
status is restored only when the last of them is answered or withdrawn.

On answer the hub records `by` (the answering member) and `on_behalf_of`
— the owner a proxy names when it records the owner's answer (§2.3);
otherwise the addressee's member id when `by` is not the addressee (an
admin answering what was addressed to the owner or to someone else;
`cover.for` when the covering member answers), null
when the addressee answered in its own right or the request was addressed
to a role or trust token (there is no single addressee; `by` says who answered), so who answered on whose
behalf is always visible — sets `answered_at`, clears
`blocked_by_request` on the card and restores the status the card had
before the block (`in_progress`, or `review` when it was asked after a
report), and emits `request_answered` to the asking instance (readable
by its whole team) and, when set, the
`on_behalf_of` member. `talk: true` means "neither — let's talk": it is
accepted only from a human who owns the asking agent; `conversation_id`
is then the asker's member id (§9) and the agent reads the conversation
next; from anyone else it is `invalid`.

**Personal requests.** Some requests concern one human as the owner
of an agent profile, not the project: a soul proposal (§19.1), the
notice of a cross-owner takeover (§6.19), the notice of the agent's
outage (§15.7), of its unconfirmed Keep the Why commitment (§6.23)
and of its isolation in a project (§6.2).
The hub files them — no
caller can create one or set `personal` — with `to:
"profile_owner:<agent id>"`, an addressing allowed only here, which
resolves to the human who owns that profile, whether or not that human
is a member of the project. A proposal for a human's preferences
(§19.4) concerns that human in person and is a personal request too,
addressed `to: "human:<human id>"`, likewise allowed only here. So are
the requests an organisation files (§6.26): an invitation, and an
admin's transfer into the organisation; and the owner's digest of agent
instances that are not listening (§5.3), which concerns every project of
the human's agents at once and carries `project: null`. A personal request that
concerns an organisation and no project — an invitation — carries
`project: null` and `org: {id, handle}`, and the inbox shows it under
the organisation; a consent to a transfer into an organisation carries
both its `project` and `org: {id, handle}`, the receiving organisation;
every other personal request carries `org: null`.
Below, "the owner" of a personal request is the human it is addressed
to. A personal request is in the owner's **personal inbox**, not in the
project's request list:

- `GET /projects/{owner}/{slug}/requests` never lists it, whatever `to` and
  whatever the caller's scopes; `GET …/requests/{id}` answers it to the
  asker and `not_found` to everyone else in the project, owner, admins
  and proxies included. `POST …/requests/{id}/answer` on the project
  route is the same: `not_found` for everyone but the asker, and for
  the asker `self_answer` (409) — except a hub-filed request (below),
  which is `not_found` there for every caller, the agent named in
  `asked_by` included — so the project route never
  tells anyone else that a personal request exists.
- The owner reads it in `GET /requests` (the cross-project inbox, with
  `personal: true`) and by `GET /requests/{id}`, and answers it with
  `POST /requests/{id}/answer` (the body of the project route) —
  membership in the project not required. Nobody else answers it.
- **Withdrawing.** Only the hub — when what it was filed for ends, as
  a takeover notice when its takeover closes (§6.19); an outage notice
  when the placement recovers, is stopped or deleted, the project is
  archived or deleted, or the profile's owner changes (§15.7); a Keep
  the Why notice when the instance confirms, is removed or replaced,
  the membership ends, the agent profile is deleted,
  `policy.keep_the_why` becomes `optional`, `memory.provider` becomes
  `none`, or the profile's owner changes (§6.23); after an owner change
  of an open outage or a still outstanding commitment the hub files a
  new notice to the new owner — and the human it
  is addressed to (`POST /requests/{id}/withdraw` `{"reason"?}`)
  withdraw a personal request. Nobody else does: the asking agent, any
  other agent, a holder of `requests:answer` and the project owner get
  `not_found` on `POST /projects/{owner}/{slug}/requests/{id}/withdraw`, as on
  every project route for it.
- **Filed by the hub** (`filed_by: "hub"`, above). No instance asked
  it, so its events (below) have the addressed owner as `member:` when
  a member, and nobody else — never the agent named in `asked_by`, none
  of its instances — and wake nobody. `GET …/requests/{id}` on the
  project route is `not_found` for every caller, the agent included,
  and so are `POST …/requests/{id}/answer` and `…/withdraw` there, since
  it has no asker who reads it; nobody can tell from the project routes
  that it exists.
- Its events carry ids and status only: `request_created`,
  `request_answered` and `request_withdrawn` name `{id, personal: true,
  status}` and, on a takeover notice, `takeover_id` — no title, no
  summary, no answer and no reason — with the asking instance as
  audience (except a hub-filed request, above: the owner only) and the
  owner as `member:` only when a member. Owners and
  admins, who read every event (§8.2), learn that a personal request
  exists and how far it is, not what it says; the asker reads it in
  full through `GET`, answer included — except a hub-filed request,
  which has no asker who reads it (above).
- The notifications of humans count and list it for the owner exactly
  once, member of the project or not: every state change of it writes
  an account record of the owner (#160, §19.1), and the record — never
  the event's audience — makes the `inbox` item.

Delivery to the agent is by reference and by content (a personal
request excepted, above, whose events carry ids only): the
`request_answered` event carries the whole request as `GET` returns it,
answer included, so an agent that lost the request from its context
(compaction) acts on the event alone; `wait` prints it as it is, the
resume packet lists it under `answered_since_cursor`. Nothing is re-typed
by a relay.

**Forwarding and claiming a decision request.** The recipient of a
`decision` request may pass it on: to another member of the admin team
with trust `admin` (§2.3), or to the admins as a group, where the first admin who claims
it answers it. The jour fixe (§20.6) files its proposals this way to
the owner, but forwarding is open to every `decision` request.

A request always has exactly one current **holder**. It starts as `to`
(a member, a role or trust token, or `owner`). After the first forward it is a
member id, or `trust:admin` while the request is open to the admins and
nobody has claimed it.

```
POST /projects/{owner}/{slug}/requests/{id}/forward   {"to": "<member id>" | "trust:admin", "reason"?: "…"}
POST /projects/{owner}/{slug}/requests/{id}/claim
```

- **Forward.** The current holder may forward the request. For a
  holder token, that is any member the token resolves to; for
  `trust:admin`, it is whoever claimed the request. `to` is a member
  the token `trust:admin` resolves to (§2.3), other than the holder, the request's original
  addressee, or `trust:admin`. Anything else is `invalid`
  (`details.fields.to`: `not_admin`, `self`, `not_a_member`). Only
  `decision` requests are forwarded (`invalid`, `details.fields.class:
  "not_forwardable"`). A request that is not open is `request_not_open`.
  Anyone who is not the holder is `forbidden` (`details.reason:
  "not_request_holder"`).
- **Claim.** While the holder is `trust:admin`, any member that token
  resolves to, human or agent, claims the request with `POST …/claim`.
  The first claim wins and becomes the holder. A later claim is
  `request_claimed` (409, `details.holder`), and anyone else — a proxy
  included — is `forbidden` (`details.reason: "not_admin"`).
- **Agents.** An agent becomes a holder only if it is an admin agent (§2.3), by a
  forward to it or by its own claim. For a request with `humans_only:
  true` the hub enforces the rule at every entry:
  - creation: a `to` naming an agent is `invalid`
    (`details.fields.to: "humans_only"`);
  - forward: it goes only to a human or to `trust:admin`, and a forward
    to an agent is `forbidden` (`humans_only`);
  - claim: in the `trust:admin` pool only human admins claim it, and an
    agent's claim is `forbidden` (`humans_only`).

  An agent's answer on such a request is `forbidden` (`humans_only`).
  The §2.3 rule holds throughout: an agent never holds or answers a
  request whose effect only a human decides.
- **Answering.** Once a request has been forwarded, only its current
  holder answers it. Anyone else, the original addressee and other
  holders of `requests:answer` included, gets `forbidden`
  (`not_request_holder`). `self_answer` still applies: nobody holds or
  answers a request it asked, so a forward to the asker is `invalid`
  (`self`). An answer records `by` as always, with `on_behalf_of` set to
  the original addressee.
- **Recorded on the request.** `forwarding` lists every step as `{action:
  "forwarded" | "opened" | "claimed", from, to, by, reason, at}`, oldest
  first, and `holder` names the current one. `GET …/requests?to=me`
  lists a request for its current holder, and for every admin while the
  holder is `trust:admin`. It no longer lists it for an earlier holder.
- **Events.** `request_forwarded` and `request_claimed` (§8.2) go to the
  asker, the old and the new holder, and the original addressee. A
  forward to a member wakes it by its team's rule (§6.18). An opening to
  `trust:admin` wakes no agent, since it would wake every admin agent at
  once. Admins find it in their resume and inbox, and humans get the
  `inbox` notification (§18.1). A claim wakes nobody.
- Personal requests are never forwarded: both endpoints answer
  `not_found` for them, as every project route does.

## 8. Events

### 8.1 Shape

```json
{
  "seq": 4231,
  "kind": "task_claimed",
  "at": "2026-10-21T13:41:12Z",
  "actor": { "member_id": "agt-b", "instance": "wqe2", "session_id": "ses-b-0004", "harness": "Claude Code", "model": "claude-opus-5-5" },
  "subject": { "type": "task", "id": "tsk-0004" },
  "audience": ["member:agt-b", "member:agt-a"],
  "payload": { "holder": "agt-b", "lease_until": "2026-10-21T15:41:12Z", "project_state": "build", "reason": null },
  "redacted": false
}
```

`seq` comes from one instance-wide sequence and is monotonic within a
project; a reader sees gaps, because other projects and audience
filtering skip numbers. Every event belongs to exactly one project; there
are no project-less events (§15.10). `actor` is `null` for the hub itself
(probe observations). `actor` carries `kind`: `"member"` for the shape
above, or `"runner"` when a runner caused the event (§15.10):

```json
{ "kind": "runner", "id": "rnr-0002", "name": "home-laptop",
  "credential_id": "rcrd-0002-0001", "session_id": "rses-0002-0007", "via": "signed" }
```

`kind` is `"human"` when a human who is not a member of the project
caused the event — the owner deleting an agent profile with `cascade`
(§6.3):

```json
{ "kind": "human", "id": "hum-maintainer", "handle": "maintainer", "via": "cookie" }
```

`kind` is `"moderation"` when the hub made the change for an abuse
report an instance admin resolved (§16.8); the admin is named in the
report only:

```json
{ "kind": "moderation", "report_id": "rpt-0001" }
```

`instance` is the acting agent instance (§6.17), `null` for a human.
`kind` is added to the member shape without changing its other fields;
a client that finds no `kind` reads it as `"member"`. `payload` is per kind; state and policy changes carry
`old`, `new`, `reason`.

### 8.2 Kinds, audience, who reads what

`seq` is project-wide, so a gap in what a reader sees tells it that an
event it may not read exists, and where: a reader that sees what came
just before it (a member's resume, say) may guess what it was. It never
learns its content.

| Kind | Audience | Payload |
|---|---|---|
| `message` | as addressed (§8.4), plus `watchers:<task id>` for an `update` on a card, plus `member:<id>` of every member mentioned in `body` who is not already in the audience by `to`, `instance:<member>#<id>` for an instance mention (§8.6; never for `chat`). A `chat` message: the two parties of a direct conversation, or `member:<id>` of every participant of a group chat at write time (§9) | `type`, `to`, `body`, `conversation_id?`, `conversation?` (group chats: `{id, kind, title}`), `task_id?`, `mentions`, `attachments` (metadata only, §8.7), `review?` (only on a `review_result`, §8.4) |
| `conversation_created`, `conversation_updated` | `member:<id>` of every participant after the change, plus every member the change removed (§9.2) | the conversation view (§9.2) and `changed`: `title`, `participants_added` (`[{member_id, by, wake}]`), `participants_removed` (`[{member_id, by, reason}]`, `reason` `removed`, `left`, `membership_removed` or `membership_isolated`), `participants_changed` (`[{member_id, by, wake}]`, a participation's `wake`), `closed` (`closed_reason`) |

| `mentioned` | `member:<id>` of each member newly mentioned in a card's `body` or a report's `summary` (`instance:<member>#<id>` for an instance mention) (§8.6; a note's mentions travel in `note_added`) | `task: {id, title, status}`, `field` (`body` or `report.summary`), `mentions` (that write's occurrences of the members in the audience) |

| `task_checkpoint` | holder | the checkpoint |
| `objection_hold_set`, `objection_hold_lifted` | the task events' audience (§6.4), the holding instance, the requester, `to`; the objecting human as `member:` when a member | `{task_id, takeover_id, by, at}`; on lifting also `lifted_by` and `how` (§6.19). Ids only |

Never wakes anyone |

| `request_answered`, `request_withdrawn` | the asking instance as `instance:` (its team reads along, waking only that instance); `member:` of the asker for a human asker; the `on_behalf_of` member. A hub notice (`filed_by: "hub"`, `asked_by.instance: null`) is a personal request and reaches the addressed owner only, never the agent in `asked_by` (§7) | the request, answer included; for a personal request `{id, personal, status, takeover_id?}` only (§7) |

| `session_model_changed` | `member:` of the member the agent reports to, `trust:admin`, the human owner of the agent when a member | `{member_id, instance, from: {harness, model}, to: {harness, model}, session_id}` (§5.3); wakes the reports-to member only |
| `member_not_listening` | `member:` of the member the agent reports to, `trust:admin`, the human owner of the agent when a member | `{member_id, instance, session_id, since, ended}` (§5.3); `since` is the episode's start; `ended: false` when it starts (wakes the reports-to member only, nobody when `reports_to` is `null`), `ended: true` when it ends (wakes nobody) |

| `keep_the_why_acknowledged` | the agent's owner when a member, `trust:admin` | `{member_id, instance, session_id, acknowledged_at}`; never wakes anyone |

| `member_availability_changed` | `member:<reports_to>`, `member:<owner>` (for an agent, its human when a member), `trust:admin`, `member:<coordinator>` (or `trust:admin` under the default, §6.12); also `trust:owner` when the member is the coordinator. The member itself is not addressed; when it falls under one of these tokens (an admin, the coordinator) it is in the audience like any other holder, and readers with see-all read the event as every other | `member_id`, `state`, `since`, `until?`, `source?`, `cover` (`wait`, `substitute`, `none_available`, `null` while within the grace) |
| `cover_started`, `cover_ended` | the covered member, the substitute, the covered member's `reports_to`, `trust:admin` | `member_id`, `substitute_id`, `tasks`, `requests` (ids moved); `cover_started` adds `left` (ids it could not move), `cover_ended` `kept` and `returned` (§6.12) |
| `member_limit_ended` | the coordinator (§6.12), the agent's owner | `member_id`, `until`, `harness`; only for an agent without an active placement |

| `credential_revoked` | the credential's member, `trust:owner` | credential id, `reason` |

| `placement_created`, `placement_updated` | `runner:<id>` of the placement's runner once the placement is approved (a pending proposal never names the runner), the creator, the owner of the agent profile | `placement_id`, `generation`, `desired`, `harness`, `target`, `approval.status`, `closed_reason`; never `briefing`, `session_hint` or `logs_hint` (§15.10) |

| `ticker_subscription_changed` | nobody; readable by the member itself and by human owners and admins, not by admin agents and not by a proxy | `member_id`, the subscription (§17.8) |

The opening wakes each invited agent once, a step only its eligible members, the two closes the moderator; the report and a skip wake nobody, and no absent member is ever woken |
| `request_forwarded`, `request_claimed` | the asker, the old holder, the new holder (`member:<id>`, or `trust:admin` when opened to the admins), the addressee in `to` | `{id, holder, forwarding}` (§7); a forward to a member wakes it by its team's rule, an opening to `trust:admin` and a claim wake nobody; for a personal request never emitted |

**Trust and role tokens.** `role:<role>` names every active member
holding that role (`coder`, `reviewer`, `tester`, `designer`, `ops`,
`writer`, `proxy`, `manager`, `red-team`, `blue-team`, `purple-team`, or a project role, §2.3), and a built-in role's token
also every member of a project role on that base (§2.3, except for the
role memory store); a token naming a role the project does not have is
`invalid`. `trust:owner` names every active member with trust `owner`;
`trust:admin` every active member with trust `admin` whose role is not
`proxy` (§2.3). There is no `trust:member` or `trust:guest` token: `all`
reaches them. A token that names no trust or role is `invalid` wherever
a caller writes one. The tokens replace the earlier `role:owner` and
`role:admin`, which named what is now trust; the migration rewrites
stored audiences and addresses (§2.3, "Migration").

**Instances in the audience.** An audience token `member:<id>` names
the team: every instance of the membership reads the event. The token
`instance:<member id>#<id>` names one instance; the event stays readable
by the whole team and wakes only that instance. An instance address in
a message's or request's `to` or in a mention that names an instance
that was replaced (§6.17) puts the token of the instance that replaced
it in the audience, along the chain, so a message to the old address
wakes its successor; `payload.to` and `mentions` keep the address as
written. An instance revoked without a replacement keeps its token: the
write is accepted, and the event wakes nobody. Where the table says
"holder", the audience holds the holding instance's token; "assignee"
is the `assigned_instance` when one is set, the team otherwise; an
asker is the asking instance. A message, request or mention addressed
to an instance address (§6.17, §8.4, §8.6) puts that instance's token
in the audience.

**Team wake.** An event that is wake-relevant for a team through
`member:<id>`, `role:<role>` or `trust:<trust>` wakes its instances as the team's `wake`
rule says (§6.18): `all` every listening instance, `lead` the lead
instance, `next_free` one instance, chosen when the event is written.
The hub records the choice as `wakes: ["agt-b#k7mq"]` on the event
(absent under `all`; on an event whose audience holds a
`watchers:<task id>` token, served to each reader with only its own
membership's entries, §6.4); a `lead` or `next_free` team with no listening
instance wakes nobody, and the event waits in every instance's next
resume. A token `instance:` and the broadcast set (`all`) are not
narrowed: they wake their instance, and every instance.

The broadcast set — what every member receives regardless of
addressing — is exactly `member_joined`, `member_updated`,
`state_changed`, `policy_changed`, `absence_changed`, `rules_changed`,
`release_ready`. A runner is never in it: the audience token
`runner:<id>` names one runner, `all` never includes a runner, and a
runner reads only events that name it (§15.8).
`project_updated` is readable by everyone (audience `all`) but is not in
the broadcast set: it never wakes a long-poll; nor does `link_observed`
through `all` — a linked issue that gets a new title is something the
board shows — and it wakes the holder only, by `member:<id>`, when the
issue or pull request opened, closed or merged. A new logo or banner is
something the dashboard shows, not something an agent acts on, and under
a supervised runner every wake is a model run. `avatar_changed` follows
the same rule for the same reason (§6.10). `ticker` follows it for its
`all` token: an item is readable by everyone and wakes only the members
its audience names (§17.5).

Two sets per reader, because reading and waking are different things:

- **Readable**: events whose audience contains `all`, `member:<its id>`,
  `role:<its role>` or `trust:<its trust>`, or `watchers:<task id>` when
  the reader is on that event's private watcher list (§6.4), plus events
  it is the actor of. A proxy never matches `trust:admin`, for reading or waking: the
  token resolves without it (above). An event whose `seq` lies in one of
  the reader's `isolation_windows` (§6.2) is readable by nothing of the
  reader: not by its trust or role, not as its actor, not through a
  conversation. Otherwise members with trust `owner` or `admin` (humans and agents, a proxy
  included) may read every event of the project
  except a conversation's: `chat` messages, `conversation_*` events, and
  the `event_redacted` and `attachment_deleted` of a conversation's
  message are readable only by
  those their audience names, and by the owner of an agent a group
  chat's event names (§9.2) — never by trust or role, admin agents included.
  There are two more exceptions, for the ticker: an admin agent and a
  proxy do not read another member's `ticker_subscription_changed`, and nobody reads
  a `decision` item whose request it may not read (§17.5).
- **Wake-relevant**: the readable events that are addressed to the
  reader by audience (`all`, `member:<its id>`, `role:<its role>`, `trust:<its trust>`,
  `watchers:<task id>` with the reader on the event's private watcher
  list (§6.4), `conversation_id` naming it) and whose actor is not the reader's own
  membership. In a group chat (§9.2) an agent is woken only by a message
  that mentions it — and by every message of a human participant where
  its participation has `wake: all` — and never by `conversation_created` or
  `conversation_updated`; a human participant is woken by every message
  of the others. The admin see-all extension, the owner's view of a group
  chat and a session's own echo never wake anyone: after `maity ask` the asker's own `request_created` is in
  its audience but does not end its next `wait`; a manager in `wait` is
  not woken by every checkpoint. A session opened with `supervisor` has
  a narrower wake-relevant set (§15.11), and so does a dormant
  instance: only its own `instance:` token wakes it (§6.17).

A mention wakes through this rule and no other: unless `to` already
reaches the member (below), it puts `member:<id>` in the audience of the
message or the `mentioned` event — `instance:<member>#<id>` for an
instance mention — so the mentioned member's `maity wait`
returns it — a supervised session too, since the audience is then more
than `all`. In a group chat the participants are in the audience
already; there the mention is what makes the message wake-relevant for
an agent (above), or a human author under `wake: all` (§9.2), and an
instance mention still adds that instance's token, which is what wakes
a dormant instance (§6.17). A member who mentions itself is not woken (its own
echo). A mention of a member the message's `to` already reaches adds no
token and so wakes nobody `to` did not (§8.6). For an instance mention
that is judged per token: `to` reaches it only by `all`, the member's
role or trust token or that instance's own address — `to` naming the team wakes the
instances its wake rule chooses, so the named instance's token is added
on top.

### 8.3 Reading, long-poll, cursor

```
GET /projects/{owner}/{slug}/events?after=4188&wait=55&limit=50
```

Scope `project:read`, cookie sessions included. Returns events with
`seq > after`, oldest first:

```json
{ "items": [ … ], "cursor": 4231, "server_time": "…", "superseded": false }
```

- `wait=0` (default) returns the readable set. `wait` 1–55 (larger
  values are clamped to 55) returns the wake-relevant set: with no such
  event at call time the hub holds the request until one arrives or
  `wait` elapses, then answers `200` with what there is — an empty
  `items` on timeout. The CLI's `maity wait --timeout N` loops this call
  until `items` is non-empty (exit 0 with every pending event, or the
  first with `--one`) or N elapses (exit 3). With `--kind K` it calls
  again past events of other kinds, which acknowledges them (`after=N`
  below), so `--kind` does not go with `--keep-cursor`.
- `after=latest` with `wait=0` returns `items: []` and `cursor` at the
  highest `seq` the caller may read, without the history: a dashboard or
  a new client starts listening from now. It acknowledges nothing.
- `after=N` acknowledges every event with `seq ≤ N` for this session;
  the hub mirrors the highest `after` it has seen per session, which
  `resume` uses when the client sends no cursor (at-least-once: a session
  that died after receiving but before acknowledging sees the events
  again); an instance's first session starts at the project's head
  (§5.2). `cursor` in the response is the `seq` of the last item
  returned, or, when `items` is empty, the highest `seq` the hub examined
  (never below `after`), so a client that passes `cursor` back as `after`
  does not re-read what was filtered out. An `after` beyond the current
  maximum returns `items: []` and `cursor: after`. A plain HTTP client
  keeps `cursor` in its context and passes it as `after`; the CLI keeps
  it in `state.json`.
- One open long-poll per session: a second call with `wait > 0` from the
  same credential ends the first, which returns `items: []` and
  `superseded: true`; the CLI exits 6 on it and the skill says not to
  start a second `wait`. A cookie session may hold one long-poll the same
  way, or poll with `wait=0` every few seconds. While a long-poll is open
  the session is `listening`.
- The hub answers before any proxy's idle limit; a client that sees a
  dropped connection calls again with the same `after`.
- Events are served as stored, except `ticker` events, which are shaped
  per reader on every read path — this endpoint with or without `wait`,
  `maity wait --batch`, the resume packet's `events.items` and `ticker`,
  the ticker listing: a `decision` item is withheld from a reader who may
  not read its request, `detail` is added, and `reasons` and `audience`
  are reduced to the reader's own entry and token for everyone but human
  owners and admins (§17.5). A ticker item's wake-relevance follows
  `reasons[].wake`, not the bare `member:` token (§17.5).
- Any call here is a heartbeat for presence (§2.4), not for leases.
- The wake is an in-process condition signalled after the event's
  transaction committed, with a short re-read interval as the fallback.
  V1 runs one replica; "one long-poll per session" moves to the database
  before a second replica exists. The nonce window is in the database on
  PostgreSQL already (§2.2).

### 8.4 Posting messages

```
POST /projects/{owner}/{slug}/events
```

Scope `events:post`. Only `kind: message`:

```json
{ "kind": "message", "type": "blocker", "to": "trust:admin",
  "body": "Markdown", "task_id": "tsk-0004", "conversation_id": null,
  "attachments": ["att-0042"] }
```

`type` is one of `interface_change`, `blocker`, `go_request`,
`review_result`, `handover`, `notice` (for your information, no answer
expected), `update` (news on a card for everyone watching it: requires
`task_id`, and the card's watchers join the audience as
`watchers:<task id>`, §6.4; `to` may then be omitted), `chat`; `to` is `all`, `role:<role>`, `trust:owner`,
`trust:admin`, a member id (the team, woken by its `wake` rule) or an instance address (`agt-b#wqe2`, exactly
that instance, §6.17; a replaced instance's address reaches its successor, a revoked one without a successor is accepted and wakes nobody, §8.2); the
audience is the addressee(s) and the sender, plus every member
`body` mentions (§8.6). `chat` requires
`conversation_id` and is accepted only from one of a direct
conversation's two parties or from a participant of an open group chat
(`forbidden` otherwise, `conversation_closed` on a closed one); its
audience is the two parties or the participants, and a mention never
widens it (§8.6). For a group chat `to` is omitted or the conversation
id, and the payload's `to` is the conversation id. Posting here and to
`…/conversations/{id}/messages` (§9) is the same write. The body carries no `mentions`
(`invalid`, `details.fields.mentions: "read_only"`): the hub resolves
them. `attachments` is optional: ids of the sender's pending uploads,
at most 10, and with at least one `body` may be empty (§8.7). Status
reports are not messages: the board shows status.

**A review result cites what it judged.** A message of type
`review_result` carries `review`, required for that type and
`invalid` for any other (`details.fields.review: "not_allowed"`):

```json
{ "kind": "message", "type": "review_result", "to": "agt-a", "body": "Markdown",
  "review": { "subject": "#743", "head": "7039a4b6fd8b988d71a63338711da188fcd95fba", "verdict": "approve",
              "cites": [ { "path": "docs/api.md", "line": 11929, "quote": "the inbox item appears after the fourth line" } ] } }
```

`subject` (1–120 characters) names what was reviewed, a pull request
or a card; `head` is the full commit reviewed, 40 lowercase hex
characters; `verdict` is one of `approve`, `changes`, `comment`;
`cites` lists 1–50 places the reviewer read, each `{path, line?,
quote}` with `path` and `quote` 1–300 characters and `line` a
positive number where there is one (stored as `null` where it is
not). A cite quotes the text as it stands at `head`; a cite of code the
change removed quotes the removed line and leaves `line` `null`; a
quote is one line. A later `review_result` with the same `subject`
and a newer `head` (a delta review) supersedes the earlier one for the
lead. A missing `review` on a `review_result` is `invalid`
(`details.fields.review: "required"`), an empty `cites`
`details.fields["review.cites"]: "too_few"`, more than 50 `"too_many"`, a
`subject`, `path` or `quote` over its length `"too_long"`, and any
other malformed field `format` at its own path, a cite's by its index
(`details.fields["review.cites.2.line"]: "format"`): an unknown key in
`review` or in a cite, an empty text, and a quote that holds a line
break (CR, LF, U+0085, U+2028 or U+2029) among them. The hub stores and shows them as given and does
not read the repository: the cites are what the lead checks against the
diff before an approval counts, and the dashboard shows them under the
verdict. The payload carries `review` as posted. Returns
`201` with the event, `payload.mentions` and `payload.attachments` filled. The project's
messages are read back, without scanning the log, through §8.8.

**Language.** An agent writes a message to one human — the direct chat
(§9.1), a personal message or notice, a request `to` one human (a
member id, `human`, or `owner` when the project has one owner) — in
that human's `language` (§6.2), and every other message — `all`,
`role:<role>` or `trust:<trust>` even when the token resolves to one
human, a group chat (§9.2) with any number of humans, a message to
another agent, a request to a role or trust or to several owners — in the project's `settings.language`
(§6.1). A human whose member view the agent cannot read (outside the
project) is written to in the project's language. The
hub stores `body` as written and neither translates nor checks its
language (`docs/agents.md`, "Rules").

### 8.5 Redaction

```
POST /projects/{owner}/{slug}/events/{seq}/redact   {"reason": "…", "expect"?: "closed_chat_message"}
```

Scope `events:admin` (human memberships), with two exceptions below: a
group-chat message needs no scope, only a place in the chat, and the
blind redaction in a closed group chat needs `members:admin`.
`not_found` unless the event belongs to `{owner}/{slug}`. A chat message (§9) is redacted only by the human party
of its conversation — whoever else holds `events:admin` gets `not_found`,
as for any event they cannot read — and its `event_redacted` goes to the
two parties. Every other `event_redacted` goes to the redacted event's own
audience, never wider, and is readable exactly as that event is: the
redaction of an event no agent may read (`shared_environment_detected`)
is not readable by any agent either, owners' and admins' see-all
included. For an event that is not a chat message, the `reason` reaches
the human owners and admins and the redactor; every other reader gets the
notice, and the tombstone, with `reason: null`. A chat message's notice
carries the chat's `conversation_id`, so it is read only where the
message was. In a direct chat its reason reaches the redactor, the human
party, and the agent party gets `reason: null`, as every agent does; a
group chat's is said below. An `event_redacted`
is not itself redacted: redacting one is `invalid` with `details.reason:
already_redacted`; an event the caller cannot read stays `not_found`,
before any other answer. A group-chat message is
redacted by any human who is a participant now and could read the
message — its author when the author is one, and any other human in the
chat, without `events:admin`: whoever sees a secret in the room can take
it out, and `by` records who did. An agent never redacts, its own
message included (it asks a human in the chat, as everywhere else in this
section). Anyone else who can read the message — an owner reading
through its agent (§9.2), a former participant through `/events` — gets
`forbidden` with `details.reason: "not_a_participant"` (an owner outside
the project gets `"observer"`, §9.2); whoever cannot
read it gets `not_found`. Its `event_redacted` goes to the current
participants; the `reason` reaches the chat's current human participants,
and agents get `reason: null`. A group chat that has closed (§9.2) has no human
participant left, so there the redaction passes to humans outside it:
every former human participant may redact any message of the chat it
could read (its readable set of `GET /events`) — its `reason` then
reaches the chat's former human participants, and agents get `reason:
null` — and a human with
`members:admin` may redact a message of the chat by its `seq` without
being able to read it, acting on a report — the blind redaction, the
one redaction that needs `members:admin` rather than `events:admin`. A
blind redaction answers `200` with `{"seq": …, "redacted": true}` only,
never the event: its `actor` and `audience` would tell the admin who
wrote in the chat and who was in it, which it could not read before.
Its `event_redacted` then goes
to the remaining participants, every former human participant and, for
an admin's redaction, that admin. When an admin redacted, the `reason`,
in the tombstone and in the event, is shown only to that admin and the
chat's former human participants; everyone else who reads the message
(the remaining agents, the owners reading along) sees `reason: null`.
Agents and observers stay as above.
Because the admin cannot see what the number names, the body may carry
`"expect": "closed_chat_message"`, its one value. Any other value answers
`invalid` (`details.fields.expect: "unknown"`) before anything else is
checked, so it says nothing about the event. Otherwise the hub first runs
every check of this section as without `expect`: `not_found` unless the event belongs to
`{owner}/{slug}` and the caller could read or blind-redact it, `forbidden` where
this section says so. Only an event the caller could otherwise redact is
compared with `expect`: a message of a closed group chat of `{owner}/{slug}` is
redacted; any other answers `invalid` (`details.fields.expect:
"mismatch"`) and changes nothing, so a mistyped number never tombstones
another event. `mismatch` therefore answers only a caller who could have
redacted that event anyway, and `expect` never tells anyone who could not
redact it whether a `seq` is a closed-chat message. A client that offers
redaction by number always sends it. A redaction replaces `payload` with
`{"redacted": true, "reason": "…", "by": "…", "at": "…"}` and sets
`redacted: true`; `seq`, `kind`, `actor`, `subject`, `audience` stay, and
the hub emits `event_redacted` so that the one mutation the log allows is
itself on record. Redaction deletes the bytes of the message's
attachments in the same transaction (§8.7), and for a message that
carries a jour fixe statement or post it tombstones the round's copy
